_about: Researched card facts (pre-launch writing review, 2026-10-15). sats: one per NORAD id; rockets: true lines per rocket family, picked by id. Every fact has the source it was checked against.

11.fact: The **first satellite built to measure cloud cover**. Its own spent rocket stage bumped into it after separating, setting it wobbling and spoiling the cloud pictures.

978.fact: The first **‘cartwheel’ weather satellite**: instead of spinning like a top, it rolled along its path like a wheel, letting its two TV cameras snap the clouds below.

1806.fact: It rode into space alongside **Canada’s Alouette 2** to study the charged upper air. With **no tape recorder**, it could only send data while a ground station was listening.

2201.fact: It measured **radiation high above Earth** to work out how risky common orbits would be for astronauts. It was built with **off-the-shelf parts** to keep costs down.

3035.fact: Its cameras beamed cloud photos **straight down to simple local stations** as it flew over. Each picture showed a patch of Earth about **3,100 km wide**.

3338.fact: Among its jobs: watching the slow fading of an **artificial radiation belt** left in space by **Starfish Prime**, an American nuclear test.

3890.fact: Shaped like an **ocean buoy**, it carried a small **nuclear power generator** as a test, to see whether the heat from radioactive fuel could power satellites.

6305.fact: A flying test bench for weather tools: one sensor read **cloud-top temperatures day and night**, while a **microwave scanner** mapped the faint radio glow from Earth’s surface.

10967.fact: Built to study the **oceans** from space, measuring waves, winds and sea temperatures. A massive **short circuit** ended the mission after only 105 days.

24285.fact: It took **high-speed snapshots of the northern lights** from above, collecting data nearly **100 times faster** than earlier satellites could.

26619.fact: Its **Hyperion** camera split light into **220 colour bands**, far more than an ordinary camera, to help spot crops and minerals from space.

26998.fact: Sent to study a layer of air nicknamed the **‘ignorosphere’**: too high for even the biggest balloons, yet too thick for satellites to stay in for long.

30580.fact: One of **five identical probes** sent to line up along Earth’s magnetic tail and find out what sets off sudden outbursts of the **northern lights**.

41851.fact: A tiny **target satellite**: people on the ground track it to tune their sensors for spotting small pieces of **space junk**.

41886.fact: One of eight satellites that measure **hurricane winds** by catching GPS signals bouncing off the sea. With its solar panels out it’s about the size of a **swan**.

116.fact: It shared its rocket with two other satellites, and besides solar cells it carried **SNAP-3**, the **first nuclear power source** ever used in space.

369.fact: From the first series of **US military weather satellites**. As it spun, its TV camera faced Earth once each turn and snapped clouds over an area about **1,300 km** across.

671.fact: A Navy research satellite that measured space radiation, including the slow **fading of a man-made radiation belt**. It kept sending useful data for **more than 11 years**.

731.fact: Part of a launch of the Navy’s secret **Poppy** spy satellites, which recorded **Soviet radar signals**. The public only heard their cover names.

829.fact: Launched as a pair with Elektron 4: this one mapped the **inner Van Allen radiation belt** while its partner flew higher to study the outer one.

1577.fact: Nicknamed **Porcupine**: a small ball with **12 rods**, each 7.6 metres long, sticking out in every direction so ground radars had a big target to practise on.

2119.fact: Navy crews called these **‘Oscars’**, the radio-alphabet word for O, meaning operational. Ships used its radio signal to work out their position, long before GPS.

2834.fact: Its public name described a gravity test, but it was secretly **Poppy 5D**, a Navy satellite that recorded signals from **Soviet missile-defence radars**.

4331.fact: The first of **Block 5A**, the sixth version of America’s secret military weather satellites. The name ‘DMSP’ was only given to them later.

4578.fact: A drum-shaped **Zaliv** satellite, part of Tsiklon, the Soviet Union’s **first satellite navigation system**. Users found their position from the shift in its radio signal.

5397.fact: Like other OV1 satellites, it **hitched a ride on a missile** test flight, a cheap way into space. It shared the trip with several test spheres and a **Mylar balloon**.

5729.fact: Built by Soviet engineers but carrying both **Soviet and French** instruments, it studied the air high over the Arctic to learn how **auroras** form.

6148.fact: Not a working satellite at all: it was an **800 kg dummy** shaped like a navigation satellite, sent up as a stand-in to test the rocket.

6920.fact: It had **no TV cameras**. Its series was the first to make cloud pictures using only **scanning sensors** that measure light and heat, so they worked by night as well as by day.

7274.fact: From **Meteor-1**, the Soviet Union’s first weather satellite series. Its cameras scanned a strip of Earth **1,000 km wide** in visible and infrared light.

7780.fact: It relayed phone calls, telegrams and **TV broadcasts** across the Soviet Union from a looping orbit that swung out to about **40,000 km**.

8645.fact: The 20th **Zaliv** navigation satellite. Each was a sealed, air-filled drum **3 metres tall**, kept pointing the right way by a long boom that used gravity.

9481.fact: A heavy **2,200 kg** weather satellite with two swivelling solar panels. A few of its siblings tested early **plasma thrusters**, gentle electric rocket engines.

10514.fact: A second-generation Soviet weather satellite. Besides cloud cameras, it carried a sensor that measured **radiation in space** around our planet.

11086.fact: One of the first two **Soviet ham-radio satellites**, built at the Moscow Aviation Institute. Battery trouble silenced it after only a few months.

12456.fact: From **Meteor-2**, the Soviet Union’s second generation of weather satellites. It weighed about **1,300 kg** and flew a near-polar orbit to watch most of the planet.

12998.fact: Went up with **five sister ham-radio satellites** on a single rocket. Their bodies were borrowed from a Soviet **military message satellite** design.

13113.fact: The first of its weather series to fly on the newer **Tsiklon-3** rocket, which took over launching these satellites from 1982.

13923.fact: The first in its series to carry **search-and-rescue** equipment, listening for distress beacons from planes and ships in trouble.

15099.fact: A Soviet weather satellite with **visible and infrared scanners** that watched clouds over the whole globe from about **900 km** up.

15738.fact: A **Molniya-3** satellite for ordinary civilian **phone calls and TV**. It swung out to about 40,000 km on each 12-hour loop, hovering high over the far north.

16591.fact: A **mother satellite**: it carried three secret Navy ocean-watching satellites into orbit, acting as their final rocket stage before letting them go.

17070.fact: Built from a navigation satellite that spent **8 years on display** in the Smithsonian museum. Engineers took it back and flew it to study how **auroras** disrupt radio.

18009.fact: One of a **trio of spy satellites** flying in a triangle. By comparing the radar signals each one heard, they could **pinpoint ships** at sea.

18820.fact: One of the later **Meteor-2** weather satellites. Its family flew in near-polar orbits between **850 and 950 km** up, passing over almost every part of Earth.

19336.fact: A third-generation Soviet weather satellite. Along with TV cameras it carried an infrared sensor called **Klimat**, Russian for **climate**.

20169.fact: Its booster motor failed and left it **stranded in the wrong orbit**, yet the mission still succeeded, measuring the positions of more than **100,000 stars**.

20439.fact: A **flying mailbox** for ham radio fans: it stored digital messages and passed them on later. It rode on Ariane’s **first-ever** piggyback flight for small satellites.

20508.fact: Also called **COSPAS 5**: besides helping ships navigate, it listened for **distress beacons** as part of the international search-and-rescue network.

20663.fact: An **Oko early-warning** satellite: its infrared telescope watched from a high, looping orbit for the heat of **missile launches**.

21152.fact: Soviet merchant ships found their position by measuring the **shift in its radio signal** as it passed overhead, about **1,000 km** up.

21577.fact: A **38 cm cube** built at a Berlin university. Arctic and Antarctic expeditions sent messages through it with handheld radios, and it still worked after **9 years**.

21798.fact: A military weather satellite that acted as its **own rocket stage**: a motor built into the spacecraft fired to push it into its final orbit.

22161.fact: A Swedish satellite that **photographed auroras** from above, with instruments from Sweden, Germany, Canada and the US. It rode up as a **piggyback** passenger.

22739.fact: Lost after just **12 days**: a single **screw that was too long** touched a live plate, causing a short circuit that drained its batteries.

22828.fact: South Korea’s second satellite and the first **built in Korea**. Its sister KITSAT-1 was made with help from engineers in **England**.

23439.fact: Built from a **spare military satellite**, it was the first payload of a brand-new rocket. **21 years** later its solar cells still powered its beacon in sunlight.

23607.fact: Built by a **university in Madrid**, this 44 kg box carried experiments on how **liquids behave** in weightlessness.

24753.fact: Designed to last **5 years**, this military weather satellite kept working for **22 years** before it was finally switched off.

25327.fact: An early-warning satellite whose telescope, with a mirror about **50 cm** across, watched for the heat of **rocket launches** and sent pictures to the ground in real time.

23788.fact: Gonets means **‘messenger’**. These satellites were offered to health groups to send **medical records** to remote places, holding messages and passing them on later.

24971.fact: Its main camera could **tilt sideways** to take stereo pairs for 3D maps, and could pick out details about **6 metres** across.

25485.fact: Carried calls for a Russian **military** network called Korund. Better radio tubes stretched its design life from two years to **three**.

25634.fact: A flying test lab with **nine experiments**, including an electric **arcjet thruster** and a detector that counted tiny bits of space dust and debris.

25736.fact: A test of using a satellite as a **very tall radio tower**, so soldiers with **hand-held radios** could talk far beyond the horizon.

25940.fact: Built by **China and Brazil** together. Its wide camera saw a strip of Earth about **890 km** across and covered the whole planet in about 5 days.

26061.fact: Built with student help, it was a **satellite carrier**: once in orbit it set free four smaller satellites and filmed each one leaving with **six cameras**.

26545.fact: One of Saudi Arabia’s **first two satellites**: a **23 cm cube** of about 10 kg, built in Riyadh, that relayed messages for radio amateurs.

27060.fact: A civilian cousin of a **Russian military** message satellite. It stored messages in memory and **delivered them later** as it passed over the person they were for.

27431.fact: Its twin, FY-1C, was later smashed by a Chinese **anti-satellite missile** in a 2007 test. This one carried a **10-channel scanner** to watch clouds.

27598.fact: A **58 cm cube** of about 50 kg, built by a team of **12 Australian organisations** to give the country its own small-satellite know-how.

27640.fact: Carried **WindSat**, which measured wind over the oceans, and a camera that tracked huge **eruptions from the Sun** heading our way.

27844.fact: A **1 kg cube** made at the Tokyo Institute of Technology. It tested radio links, sensors and a fold-out **solar panel**, opened by command from the ground.

27944.fact: A **21 cm brass ball** covered in **60 mirror prisms** that bounce laser beams straight back to Earth, helping scientists measure the planet’s shape.

28221.fact: China’s **first nanosatellite**, about 25 kg, built with **Tsinghua University** partly to train the country’s future space engineers.

28372.fact: First called **LatinSat**, it belonged to a planned network of 64 small satellites for **tracking vehicles and equipment** anywhere on Earth.

28479.fact: An ‘experiment’ satellite (that is what **Shiyan** means) testing **digital stereo imaging**, a way to map hills and valleys in 3D from space.

28654.fact: Its twin was **badly damaged in a factory accident** before launch. This one also carried **search-and-rescue** gear that listens for distress beacons.

28898.fact: Partly built by military academy students to test **laser communication**, but it **never separated** from its rocket, so no one could ever talk to it.

29049.fact: One of **six small Taiwan-US satellites** studying the air for weather forecasts. Built to last 5 years, they kept going for **14**.

37792.fact: After a 90-day checkup in orbit it was handed to a new owner and renamed **exactView 5**, joining a fleet that keeps track of **ships at sea**.

40019.fact: Also called **exactView 13**, it picked up the automatic **position signals** that ships broadcast, helping map vessels far out on the oceans.

29268.fact: Its camera, made with partners in Israel and Germany, could see details down to **1 metre**, helping to map the Korean peninsula and plan for **disasters**.

31124.fact: A **12 kg** message-relay satellite, part of Saudi Arabia’s plan for a fleet of **24**. It held messages in memory and passed them on later.

31490.fact: China calls it a remote-sensing satellite, but it is thought to double as a **military spy camera**, an optical partner to the radar-carrying Yaogan 1.

32382.fact: Built in Canada, it was the first commercial radar satellite to send and receive waves in **several polarizations** (directions the waves wiggle), helping tell ice, land and ships apart.

32953.fact: Its name means **‘jubilee’**: it was built to honour the **50th anniversary of Sputnik**, with parts of its radio made by students in Krasnoyarsk.

33316.fact: Nicknamed **Choros**. The five RapidEye satellites flew in a line about **19 minutes apart**, so together they could photograph a chosen spot every day.

33412.fact: Its **radar** sees through clouds and darkness. Italy used it to watch for **floods and landslides**, and its military used it too.

33497.fact: A **100 kg** test satellite that tried out new parts for future small spacecraft, such as **thin-film solar cells** and a tiny radiation meter.

35578.fact: It flew in a rare **near-equator orbit**, tilted only **9 degrees**, so it passed over Malaysia far more often than most satellites. It rode SpaceX’s small Falcon 1 rocket.

35865.fact: Carried a **radar** called Severyanin for watching **sea ice**, along with scanners that mapped clouds and measured temperature and humidity in the air.

35946.fact: Its camera could spot objects as small as **half a metre**, and it added four new colour bands, including ones called **‘coastal’** and **‘yellow’**.

36413.fact: One of a **trio** of Chinese satellites that fly together. Experts think they work like America’s NOSS spies, using **ships’ radio signals** to locate them at sea.

39239.fact: From the third of China’s satellite **triplets**. Flying close together about 1,100 km up, they are believed to keep track of **warships** at sea.

40111.fact: Part of a trio that likely **replaced** the earlier Yaogan 9 group. Like them, it is thought to watch over **ships at sea** from orbit.

36600.fact: Not a separate satellite: a box of test electronics **bolted to the rocket’s top stage**, trying out navigation gear for future **planes and spacecraft**.

36834.fact: A Chinese **radar** satellite that can see the ground through clouds. An older sibling, Yaogan 1, was destroyed by an **internal explosion** a few months before this launch.

37180.fact: Shijian 6 satellites fly in **pairs**, probing the radiation around Earth. Some experts think they may also test **eavesdropping** equipment.

37673.fact: Carried NASA’s **Aquarius** instrument, which measured how **salty** the ocean’s surface is. Argentina built the spacecraft, and it worked for **4 years**.

37849.fact: The only part kept when a giant US weather-satellite project was **cancelled** in 2010. Its five instruments went on to help with **everyday forecasts**.

38011.fact: Nicknamed **FASat-Charlie**. Chilean engineers trained alongside its European builders so Chile could **fly it from home**.

38339.fact: A **50 cm cube** testing new space tech, including a receiver that picked up the **identity signals ships broadcast**, heard all the way from orbit.

38736.fact: An upgraded **Gonets** messenger satellite built to last 5 to 7 years. It collects data from remote users and **drops it off** at ground stations later.

38782.fact: Venezuela’s **first remote-sensing satellite**, renamed **Francisco Miranda** in 2012. It was built in China to help monitor crops, cities and disasters.

39030.fact: Turkey’s spy satellite was **built in Turkey**, except for its camera, which came from South Korea. It can see details about **2.5 metres** across.

39090.fact: Carried an **Android smartphone** that was meant to help run the satellite, plus a tiny thruster fuelled by **water and alcohol**.

39160.fact: Its name stands for **Vietnam Natural Resources, Environment and Disaster** monitoring. It sees details about **2.5 metres** across to track climate change and disasters.

39265.fact: Carried **Cascade**, a test ‘space courier’ meant to pick up big data parcels at the end of a work day and deliver them across the world by the next morning.

39418.fact: Built in-house by start-up **Skybox Imaging**, this 83 kg satellite used **camera chips** like those in phones to see details about **1 metre** across.

39426.fact: One of three identical **CubeSats** built with students in California and South Korea to make **stereo movies** of energetic atoms swirling around Earth.

39440.fact: Nicknamed **Manolito**, this tiny Argentine satellite tested **open-source** designs anyone could reuse, then became a relay for ham radio fans.

39453.fact: One of **three** satellites mapping Earth’s **magnetic field** to learn about the planet’s insides. It flies side by side with its twin, Swarm A, lower than their sister Swarm B.

39492.fact: Built by students and scientists at **Samara University**, it measured Earth’s magnetic field and counted hits from **tiny bits of space dust**.

39762.fact: A military **store-and-forward** satellite: it records messages as it flies over the sender, then plays them back when it reaches the receiver.

40011.fact: A 64 kg satellite from the **University of Tokyo** with its own **ion engine** and a camera that could see details down to **5 metres**.

40037.fact: A small **6U CubeSat** that listened for the **identity signals ships broadcast** to track them at sea. Its makers had first planned to give it a camera.

40056.fact: Built at the **University of Toronto**, it practised **formation flying** with its twin CanX-4, using GPS to measure the gap between them to within **10 cm**.

40071.fact: The **first Russian satellite paid for entirely by private money**. The 27 kg box tested new parts and carried a receiver for tracking ships.

40275.fact: The fourth satellite in a new generation of Chinese **optical spy satellites**, which fly about **1,200 km** above the ground.

40358.fact: The first **Lotos-S1** satellite, part of a Russian system called Liana that **listens in on radio signals** from orbit.

40697.fact: Its camera sees in **13 colour bands** and photographs a strip of land **290 km** wide, used to map farms, forests and how land changes over time.

40894.fact: Its sharp camera can see things **smaller than a metre**, used for planning cities and roads and settling **who owns land**.

40959.fact: Shoots **4K colour video** of the ground instead of single snapshots, sharp enough to show things about **1.3 metres** across.

41166.fact: Built at Singapore’s **Nanyang Technological University**, it studied tropical weather by watching **GPS signals bend** as they passed through the air.

41456.fact: Its **radar** was built to see through clouds and darkness along a strip up to **700 km** wide. A power failure ended Sentinel-1B’s mission in 2021; ESA announced its retirement in 2022.

41634.fact: Reported to study **radiation** in space and how it affects equipment. It flies in the same tilted orbit, about **75 degrees**, as its twin SJ 16-01.

41784.fact: Built by a research lab at a **college in Bangalore**, this 5 kg nanosatellite carried a small **colour camera** made in Denmark.

41900.fact: Its camera splits light into about **148 colour channels**, and a single satellite could scan **2.5 million square km** of ground in a day.

43229.fact: Built from **satlets**, small modules that snap together like building blocks to make a satellite. It hitched a ride beside a big Spanish TV satellite.

44493.fact: Built to serve for **15 years**, it ran into trouble right after launch and was left stuck in its **transfer orbit**, never reaching its parking spot in space.

46460.fact: Launched in a bundle of **nine** Jilin-1 satellites: some take sharp photos and others shoot **colour video** of the ground, from a few hundred km up.

48957.fact: Flies in a small group that works together to **pinpoint radio signals** on Earth, from ships to **emergency beacons**.

51102.fact: Its name means **‘Experiment 13’**: one of China’s Shiyan test satellites. China has said almost nothing about what it tests.

54253.fact: Rode into space on **Ceres-1**, a small rocket from a private Chinese company, together with four sister camera satellites.

55103.fact: A 2 kg CubeSat designed at **Kuwait University** to test whether its **colour camera** could also help it work out which way it was pointing.

58262.fact: Ordered by the government of **Andalusia** in Spain to watch **wildfires, floods and farmland**, using **AI** on board to process its pictures in space.

58309.fact: A Planet **Dove**: a **5 kg** satellite about the size of a loaf of bread with a tiny telescope inside. Doves in this kind of orbit last about **2 to 3 years**.

59908.fact: A Europe-Japan mission carrying both a **laser** and a **cloud radar** to measure clouds and dust layer by layer. Japan gave it the name **Hakuryu**.

61753.fact: A small CubeSat from Moscow’s **Bauman** technical university. Its family studies **space weather** and cosmic rays and tests tiny **plasma thrusters**.

61774.fact: One of dozens of small **SITRO-AIS** CubeSats that catch the **identity signals ships broadcast** and pass them to the ground to keep sailing safer.

62190.fact: Flies a **low, tilted orbit** to pass over mid-latitude seas more often, with a **radar** that sees through clouds and a camera for spotting **night lights**.

62402.fact: Follows Djibouti 1A, the country’s first satellite, designed by **ten Djiboutian students** trained in France to collect data from weather and earthquake stations.

65268.fact: Believed to be one of a new batch of Russian **spy camera satellites**, launched **four at a time** on one rocket, each weighing about 520 kg.

67254.fact: Works as a **pair** with Aist-2T 1, taking **stereo pictures** to build 3D maps of the land and keep watch on fires, floods and volcanoes.

100092.fact: Part of a planned Russian **space internet** network. These satellites talk to each other with **lasers** and steer with **krypton**-powered electric thrusters.

1314.fact: The **first nuclear reactor** ever switched on in orbit, and the first **ion engine** too. The reactor ran for 43 days before an electrical part failed.

2674.fact: Covered in **corner-cube mirrors** that bounced laser beams back to the ground, letting scientists pin down its position to map Earth’s shape. Its twin followed a week later.

58823.fact: Rode into space on a **Kinetica-1** rocket together with four other **Taijing** satellites from the Beijing space company Minospace.

7530.fact: Its batteries died in 1981, but in 2002 one shorted battery broke open and it **came back to life** after 21 years, running on **sunlight alone**, so it only works in daylight.

26113.fact: It went silent in 2005. In 2018 a **radio amateur in British Columbia**, hunting for a secret spy satellite, picked up its signal: IMAGE was **alive after 12 years**.

23179.fact: Nadezhda means **‘hope’** in Russian, a fitting name: these satellites listened for **distress signals** from ships and aircraft and passed them on to rescuers.

53446.fact: Trackers call it ‘**Object C**’ until they can say exactly which satellite it is. It came from a launch carrying a big batch of **Jilin-1** camera satellites.

56749.fact: Its exact identity is still unconfirmed. It came from a launch of **Nuri**, South Korea’s rocket, which carried eight small satellites; some **failed to separate**.

60745.fact: Not yet matched to a name. It came from a **Ceres-1S** rocket launched from a ship, which carried three **Yunyao-1** weather satellites and three others.

68206.fact: Still waiting to be matched to its real name. It came from a **Kuaizhou-11** rocket that carried **eight** small Chinese satellites at once.

62691.fact: Came from **Transporter-12**, a SpaceX ‘rideshare’ flight that carried **dozens** of small satellites for customers around the world, like a bus with many passengers.

69794.fact: Built by **Harvard undergraduates** and released from the space station. It aims its solar panels with **shape-memory metal** coils instead of motors.

20.fact: It mapped **Earth’s magnetic field** and found the bottom edge of the **Van Allen radiation belts**. Its rocket stage was left attached on purpose, and it should stay up for about 300 years.

117.fact: Two satellites stuck together: **Injun 1**, built at the University of Iowa, never came apart from Solrad 3 after launch. The pair should stay in orbit for about **900 years**.

397.fact: Shaped like an **18-sided drum** and covered in about **9,000 solar cells**. Its wide-angle TV camera kept sending pictures of clouds back to Earth for more than a year.

694.fact: There was no satellite on board: the **rocket stage itself** was the test. The first Centaur flight failed in 1962, so this was the **first Centaur to reach orbit**.

734.fact: One of America’s first **military weather satellites**. It spun like a top and took a cloud picture each time its camera faced Earth, covering a square about **1,300 km** on each side.

870.fact: A **topside sounder**: it fired radio signals down at the **ionosphere**, the electric layer of air that bounces radio waves, to study it from above. Its longest antennas stretched 18 metres.

1208.fact: A box about 35 cm long, almost **covered in solar cells**. Ground stations bounced radio signals off it to pin down the exact positions of faraway places, like **remote Pacific islands**.

1315.fact: Part of a US Army system that measured distances by bouncing radio signals off satellites, a step on the road to **GPS**. This one was unlucky: its radio **transponder failed**.

1580.fact: Behind the code name was a secret **military weather satellite**: the first of the Air Force’s DSAP Block 2 series, which carried improved **infrared** heat sensors.

1814.fact: It was meant to be **France’s first satellite**, but Astérix beat it to orbit by **ten days**. It listened to very low-pitched radio waves travelling through the space around Earth.

2121.fact: Carried growing **algae and duckweed** to test how plants could help keep astronauts alive. It and OV1-5 were the first two satellites put into orbit **side by side**.

3891.fact: Hitched a ride to space with the **Nimbus 3** weather satellite. Its other name, EGRS, means **Electronic and Geodetic Ranging Satellite**: it helped pin down exact spots on Earth.

2389.fact: Its radio receiver helped locate the **plasmapause**, the outer edge of the bubble of charged gas that wraps around Earth. It also measured **space radiation** that can damage spacecraft.

2680.fact: Carried **144 corner mirrors** that bounce laser light straight back to the ground, helping scientists measure the shape of Earth. Its twin, Diadème 1, went up just **one week** earlier.

2847.fact: Its name means **time and navigation**. It carried a very steady clock and helped prove that timed radio signals from space could tell you where you are: the idea behind **GPS**.

3047.fact: The very first satellite of **Tsiklon**, the Soviet Union’s first **navigation satellite system**. Users worked out where they were from the way its radio signal changed pitch as it passed.

3345.fact: Just three days after launch it photographed **Tropical Storm Shirley** over the Pacific. ESSA was named after its owner, the **Environmental Science Services Administration**.

4257.fact: Shared its rocket with **nine other satellites**. Like Timation 1, it tested ultra-steady clocks in orbit, work that paved the way for the **GPS** navigation in your phone.

4362.fact: Looked like an **ocean buoy**, nearly 3.7 metres tall. One of its instruments measured the **ozone layer** around the whole globe, and its experiments ran for more than ten years.

4783.fact: A Soviet **ionosphere sounder** that fired radio pulses down at the electric layer of air beneath it. Its twin was lost when its rocket failed, so this was the **only one** to reach orbit.

5398.fact: Just a **hollow aluminium ball** about 1.1 metres wide, with no electronics at all. Radar stations aim at it to check their accuracy, because they know **exactly how big** it should look.

5731.fact: It carried a **plasma thruster**, an engine that pushes with a stream of electrically charged gas. Meteor 1-10 was the first of four Soviet weather satellites chosen to test one.

6173.fact: Three boxes joined by booms, powered by a **nuclear battery**. A ball **floating freely** inside let it feel the drag of thin air, and tiny thrusters cancelled that drag out.

6350.fact: Not a working satellite at all: an **800 kg dummy** built like a Soviet navigation satellite and flown in its place to test the **Kosmos-3M** rocket.

6938.fact: A small **subsatellite** that rode into space on a giant **KH-9 Hexagon** spy satellite, then fired two little rockets to climb to its own orbit. Its exact job has never been made public.

7276.fact: Its two antennas sat on **telescopic arms** and tracked Earth, while its six solar panels stayed pointed at the Sun. Molniya-2 satellites carried **government messages** across the Soviet Union.

7531.fact: **Spain’s first satellite**. About 40 ground stations listened to its radio beacon to study the ionosphere, and a **killer timer** switched it off after two years.

7937.fact: Released from a giant **KH-9 Hexagon** spy satellite, it fired two small rockets to climb to its own orbit about **1,390 km** up. It is thought to have listened for **radar signals**.

8709.fact: Japan’s first **ionosphere sounding** satellite, built to forecast when **shortwave radio** would work best. A power failure stopped it after a month, so a replacement, Ume 2, followed.

9661.fact: A second-generation Soviet weather satellite weighing about **1,300 kg**. Besides watching clouds, it carried a sensor that measured **radiation** in the space around Earth.

10539.fact: A **stand-in**: it copied a Soviet eavesdropping satellite so engineers could test the new **Tsiklon-3** rocket. It was the third of four of these test dummies.

10991.fact: The **26th and last** Zaliv satellite of Tsiklon, the first Soviet **navigation system**. Users found their position from how its radio signal changed pitch as it passed overhead.

11165.fact: Officially called **Astrofizika**, yet no astronomy results were ever published. Reports suggest it watched for **artificial lights** on Earth, possibly as part of laser tests.

12458.fact: Used **pulsed plasma thrusters**, tiny electric engines, to cancel out air drag so its path stayed predictable for navigators. A **6-metre boom** kept it pointing at Earth.

12999.fact: Carried a **robot operator**: radio hams could call it in Morse code and it would answer by itself with a contact number. It was one of **six radio satellites** launched on a single rocket.

13295.fact: A Soviet **early-warning** satellite. From a long looping orbit, its telescope, with a mirror about **50 cm** wide, watched for the infrared heat of **missile launches**.

14064.fact: A Soviet **ocean spy** that tracked warships by listening to their **radar and radio signals**. Its sister satellites ran on nuclear reactors, but this type used **solar power**.

15199.fact: Worked with German and British spacecraft. The German one released clouds of **lithium and barium** in space, and this one watched for those tracer atoms drifting into Earth’s **magnetic bubble**.

15935.fact: Not a radio-ham satellite: it’s a US Navy **Transit** navigation satellite, nicknamed Oscar. This was the first **stacked Oscars** launch, two satellites on one rocket, so spares could wait in orbit.

16631.fact: One of three **NOSS** ocean-watching satellites that flew in a **triangle formation**. Together they pinpointed ships from their radar signals and even worked out their speed and direction.

17191.fact: Once a Soviet eavesdropping satellite, it later became **space junk**. In 2012 NASA’s **Fermi** gamma-ray telescope had to move out of its way to avoid a crash.

18010.fact: Flew in a team of three, spaced **30 to 240 km** apart. By comparing the radar signals each one heard, the team could work out where a ship was. A long boom kept its antennas facing Earth.

18822.fact: It doubled as its own rocket: a built-in **Star-37 motor** pushed it into its final orbit, so the satellite acted as the **last stage** of its launcher.

19419.fact: A US Navy **Transit** navigation satellite. Oscar is radio code for O, for **operational**. When GPS took over in 1996, it kept transmitting and got a new job watching the **ionosphere**.

20261.fact: Nicknamed **Aktivny**, it beamed very low-pitched radio waves into space from a huge loop antenna using a **10 kW transmitter**, while a small Czech satellite, Magion 2, flew nearby to listen.

20440.fact: DOVE stands for **Digital Orbiting Voice Encoder**: this little cube could **talk**, sending its readings as spoken messages in a computer voice for schools to listen to.

20510.fact: Its sideways-looking **radar** scanned a strip of sea **450 km wide**, so a single Okean could watch ice and water across the whole **Russian Arctic** every 3 to 5 days.

20670.fact: The United States kept separate weather satellites for the military and for forecasters, but the Soviet Union used **one type for both**. Meteor 2-19 was one of these **shared** weather watchers.

21232.fact: A third-generation Soviet weather satellite of about **2,200 kg**. Along with TV cameras, it carried an infrared sensor called **Klimat**, Russian for climate.

21578.fact: Built by a French amateur club to study **low-frequency radio waves from Jupiter** that Earth’s ionosphere blocks. Its six antennas were each **10 metres** long.

21819.fact: The only Soviet science satellite launched in 1991. It fired **beams of electrons** into the space around Earth, while a small Czech satellite, **Magion 3**, flew alongside to measure the effects.

22178.fact: Molniya means **lightning**. The Soviet Union and then Russia launched **164** of these satellites between 1965 and 2004, nearly all on the same long, looping kind of orbit.

22782.fact: Carried a unique **Fizeau mirror array**. Scientists on the ground bounced **laser beams** off it to measure exactly how far away it was.

22829.fact: **Portugal’s first satellite**. Seven Portuguese engineers learned how to build satellites by working on it alongside experts at England’s **University of Surrey**.

23189.fact: A test model for **Obzor**, a Russian Earth-watching satellite series that was **never built**. Its camera could pick out things about 75 metres across.

23455.fact: Besides watching the weather, it collected readings from **ocean buoys and drifting balloons** around the world, and relayed **distress calls** from ships and planes to rescuers.

23657.fact: Chile’s first satellite, FASat-Alfa, was meant to separate from it after launch but **never came loose**. The two satellites are **stuck together** in orbit.

23789.fact: Gonets means **messenger**. It was one of the first three working Gonets, a system offered to help health workers send **medical records** to and from remote places.

24292.fact: A short circuit in its solar panels cut it off **one day after launch**. Engineers kept calling for 20 months, and in **May 1998** it finally woke up and went back to work.

24827.fact: A Russian spy satellite with a **1.5-metre telescope**, built on a design that came from **Mars and Venus probes**. Its battery failed right after launch, but it still worked for four months.

25023.fact: A **5-metre-tall dummy** on the second Ariane 5 flight. Its **34 sensors** recorded the shaking and noise of launch, and student experiments called TEAMSAT rode along with it.

25338.fact: The first of NOAA’s **fifth generation** of polar weather satellites. It added new **microwave sensors** to measure temperature and water vapour at different heights in the air.

25489.fact: Tested **29 new technologies** at once, including Russian-designed electric thrusters and the biggest solid-state memory flown in space at the time: **51 gigabits**.

25635.fact: **Denmark’s first satellite**, named after Hans Christian Ørsted, who discovered in 1820 that **electricity creates magnetism**. Fittingly, it measured Earth’s magnetic field.

25756.fact: The first satellite **designed entirely in South Korea**, renamed **Uribyol 3** once in orbit. It was also one of the first paying passengers on India’s PSLV rocket.

25941.fact: A 60 kg science satellite meant to study **plasma bubbles** high in the atmosphere and the faint **airglow** of the night sky. Contact was lost soon after launch.

26063.fact: A **mothership** built by Stanford students: once in orbit it pushed out **six tiny satellites**. It flew on the first Minotaur rocket, made from an old Minuteman missile.

26365.fact: A **657 kg stand-in** for an Iridium phone satellite. It flew on the first Rokot-KM launch so engineers could test the rocket’s new **Briz-KM** upper stage.

26546.fact: Built to collect readings from **water, gas and power plants**, store them, and hand them on when it flew over the right ground station: a **space postman** for data.

26620.fact: Flew in a parade with **Landsat 7, EO-1 and Terra**: all four passed over the same places within an hour of each other, so scientists could compare their views.

27001.fact: Carried an American instrument, **SAGE III**, which measured the **ozone layer** and tiny dust particles in the air. It was a joint mission of the Russian and US space agencies.

27367.fact: Its name means **wings**. It tested whether everyday **commercial computer chips**, solar cells and computers could survive the harsh radiation of space.

27453.fact: Switched off in 2013. Eight years later, in March 2021, it **broke apart** into about **100 pieces** of space junk, probably because an old battery burst.

27599.fact: Built to track **whales**. The plan was for tags to record position, dive depth and water temperature, then send the data up when a whale **surfaced** beneath the satellite.

27643.fact: Searched for the glow of **million-degree gas** around the Sun’s neighbourhood and found surprisingly little. It was also the first US mission run using **internet protocols**.

27845.fact: A 3 kg **CubeSat** built with Stanford students. It listened for faint **magnetic signals** that some scientists think come before earthquakes, hoping to make quake forecasts possible.

27945.fact: Carried a **far-ultraviolet** camera to study glowing gas in space. It shared its rocket with satellites from **Turkey, Nigeria and Britain**, plus three Russian ones.

28230.fact: Its four gyroscopes were quartz balls so round they were within **40 atoms** of a perfect sphere. Spinning in **super-cold helium**, they tested Einstein’s idea that Earth twists space around it.

28373.fact: A 12 kg satellite built at **Sapienza University of Rome** to test ordinary, non-space equipment in orbit, such as new **triple-layer solar cells** and a magnetometer.

28485.fact: Named for its speed: when it spots a **gamma-ray burst**, it turns itself to look in about **20 to 75 seconds**. It was later renamed after its lead scientist, **Neil Gehrels**.

28737.fact: China launched it **without any advance notice**. Officially it was a small experimental satellite sent to **monitor the space environment** and run tests for three years.

28908.fact: The first **Strela-3M** military messenger. Like a flying mailbag, it **records messages** as it passes one station and plays them back over another. A civilian twin shared its rocket.

29050.fact: One of six COSMIC satellites that used **GPS signals** to measure the air for weather forecasts. A faulty **solar panel** weakened it in 2007, and it stopped working in 2010.

29479.fact: Hinode means **sunrise**. Its orbit follows the line between day and night on Earth, so it can watch the **Sun almost non-stop**.

30797.fact: One of five THEMIS probes studying the space storms that make **auroras** suddenly flare up. Two of its siblings were later sent to orbit the **Moon**, but this one stayed near Earth.

31125.fact: A 12 kg microsatellite that **stores messages** and delivers them later as it flies over. Saudi Arabia’s KACST institute built it, and planned a fleet of **24** like it.

31598.fact: COSMO-SkyMed stands for **Constellation of Small Satellites for Mediterranean basin Observation**. This was the first of four radar satellites watching for **floods and landslides**.

32783.fact: Rode up with **nine other satellites**, including two from Canada, CanX-2 and CanX-6. Its camera could spot things about **1 metre** across.

32958.fact: The first of China’s second generation of **polar weather satellites**. It carried a dozen instruments, from microwave sounders to an **ozone** sensor, and weighed about 2,250 kg.

33320.fact: Huanjing means **environment**. Besides its own cameras, it carried a shared payload for **seven countries**: China, Iran, South Korea, Mongolia, Pakistan, Thailand and Bangladesh.

33433.fact: A 204 kg test satellite for **stereo mapping**: photographing the ground from different angles to measure the **height of hills and valleys**.

33498.fact: Two satellites on a **tether**: mother Ku and daughter Kai, which talked by **Bluetooth**. The plan was to unreel a 10 m tether, but it only came out a few tens of centimetres.

35636.fact: Built to pick up **distress beacons** for search and rescue teams. Sadly, a control fault meant its solar panels couldn’t face the Sun, and it **ran out of power**.

35866.fact: Meant to relay **SOS signals** from people in trouble. Unlike older Russian rescue satellites it was small enough to ride along with others, but its **stabilising boom** never unfolded.

35951.fact: Earlier DMSP satellites finished the climb to orbit with their own motor, but this one rode a bigger rocket **straight into orbit**. It carried **ultraviolet** imagers to study the upper air.

36414.fact: One of a **trio** launched on one rocket to fly together. Experts think they are China’s version of the US **NOSS** ocean-watching satellites, tracking ships from orbit.

36827.fact: Tango was the **target**: a 40 kg satellite whose partner, Mango, practised chasing it, flying around it and meeting it in space. Tango’s job was simply to be chased.

37153.fact: Strela means **arrow**. These military satellites work like **mailboxes** in the sky, and this was one of the last Strela-3s, a design first launched in 1985.

37206.fact: A big TV satellite that never got to work: a **fuel leak** appeared right after launch and it was declared a **total loss**. One broken fuel pipe was the likely cause.

37730.fact: Its purpose has **never been revealed**. Oddly, it launched about three weeks **before** SJ-11-02, so the numbers in this secret series are out of order.

37793.fact: It has gone by several names, including **exactView 6** and **Myriota 2**. Besides picking up ships’ position signals, it **stores messages** and passes them on later.

37875.fact: Probably a military **optical spy** satellite, the second of three in its series. A small extra satellite, **Tianxun-1**, hitched a ride on the same rocket.

38012.fact: Sees details as small as **70 cm** and can swivel fast to snap several pictures in one pass. It teams up with Italy’s **COSMO-SkyMed** radar satellites.

38340.fact: A 7 kg university satellite that tested a **high-voltage solar panel**, and how that high voltage made the satellite build up **electric charge** in space.

38745.fact: Stranded in a useless orbit when its rocket’s **Briz-M** stage shut down after just **7 seconds** of an 18-minute burn. Indonesia’s Telkom-3 was lost on the same flight.

38860.fact: Tested Chinese **ion and Hall thrusters**, engines that push with a stream of electrically charged gas. Its twin, **SJ-9B**, launched on the same rocket.

39057.fact: A **flying post office** for the Russian military: it records messages over one station and delivers them over another. It went up with **two siblings**, Kosmos 2483 and 2484.

39091.fact: **Austria’s first satellite**, built in Toronto. It is one of six BRITE cubes that measure tiny changes in the light of the **brightest stars** in the sky.

39161.fact: **Estonia’s first satellite** and the first ever to try an **electric solar sail**, a tether meant to be pushed by the solar wind. Sadly, the tether never unreeled.

39240.fact: Part of China’s third **trio** of satellites flying together about **1,100 km** up. Experts think these trios track ships at sea, like the American NOSS satellites.

39267.fact: Built by **University of Colorado** students to measure **air drag** high above Earth. A fault stopped it taking commands, so the team measured drag by watching its **orbit change**.

39419.fact: **Sixteen Emirati engineers** helped build it in South Korea. It can see details about **1 metre** across and uses a small electric **Hall thruster** to adjust its orbit.

39427.fact: A **CubeSat** about the size of a shoebox, testing a new receiver for ships’ **position signals**. Radio hobbyists could get free software to decode what it heard.

39442.fact: A satellite that carried a satellite: it rode up inside Italy’s UniSat-5, then released its own **tiny passenger**, Pocket-PUCP, which was just **8 cm long**.

39455.fact: Officially sent up for **technological experiments and environmental surveys**, but China never described the satellite itself. It circles about **740 km** up, passing near both poles.

39574.fact: Its radar uses **two frequencies**, so it can map storms in **3D** and even estimate the size of raindrops and snowflakes. It leads a fleet that maps the world’s rain every 2 to 3 hours.

39763.fact: Useful where there are no phone lines: this military satellite picks up messages such as **faxes and emails** as it passes one station and drops them off at another, far away.

40012.fact: A satellite that delivered satellites: about **25 hours** after launch it pushed out **four CubeSats** and took pictures of them leaving with its own camera.

40020.fact: A **20 cm cube** with a tiny telescope that tracks how the **brightest stars** flicker. It measures their light at least **ten times** more precisely than telescopes on the ground can.

40039.fact: A small **6U CubeSat** that picked up ships’ position signals. It was built by an American offshoot of a Russian company, and at first it was meant to carry a **camera** instead.

40057.fact: Designed, built and run by **students** at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University. It carried a **quantum physics** experiment and a camera that could see things 20 metres across.

40072.fact: Built by **Skybox Imaging**, a start-up that Google bought and later sold to Planet. SkySats can film **video** of Earth up to **90 seconds** long, sharp enough to see cars.

40115.fact: Archaeologists used its pictures to hunt for a possible **Viking settlement** in Newfoundland, and scientists use them to **count elephants** in Africa from space.

40286.fact: The eighth of a **secret** Chinese series. Experts guess they may watch for missile launches or listen to radio signals. One of its siblings was lost when its **rocket failed**.

40362.fact: Believed to be a military **optical spy** satellite. It was launched about **490 km** up, in an orbit like the earlier Yaogan 5 series, which ended after just three launches.

40701.fact: Officially it helps with **maps, disaster response, farming and city planning**. Curiously, it flies in almost the same orbit as Yaogan-26, which is thought to be a **spy satellite**.

40905.fact: One of **20 small satellites** carried on the **first ever launch** of China’s Long March 6 rocket. Which one it is hasn’t been matched up, so it’s still listed as Object G.

40960.fact: Part of **Jilin-1**, China’s first home-grown commercial Earth-imaging fleet, named after Jilin Province. It was one of the fleet’s first **video satellites**, on its very first launch.

41167.fact: An 80 kg satellite from the **National University of Singapore** that sees in **many shades of light** beyond what eyes can, to help watch over land, water and forests in its region.

41457.fact: Tested whether **everything falls the same way** by letting two metal cylinders fall together in orbit. Einstein passed, in a test about **100 times** more precise than any on Earth.

41727.fact: Weighs about **2,950 kg** and was designed to last **eight years**. Its radar can pick out details just a few metres across, and two more Gaofen-3 satellites later joined it.

41785.fact: **Eighteen Algerian engineers** assembled and tested it in Algeria. Its launch was the first time India’s PSLV rocket dropped satellites off in **different orbits**.

41852.fact: A 3 kg **CubeSat** testing a tiny **electrospray thruster**, which pushes by spraying out electrically charged particles, plus wiring made of **carbon nanotubes**.

41887.fact: Measures **hurricane winds** by catching **GPS signals** that bounce off the rough sea. With its solar panels open, each of the eight CYGNSS satellites is about the size of a **swan**.

41901.fact: This 43 kg satellite splits light into **148 colours** to study the ground. One satellite could scan **2.5 million square kilometres** a day, about a quarter of the size of Canada.

43236.fact: Its name means **Land Surveying Satellite**, but it is likely military. It was the last of **four** sent up in just three and a half months.

44499.fact: Its 24 cm telescope sees things about **1 metre** across, and it can take up to **1,000 pictures a day**. It rode a small **Electron** rocket from New Zealand.

46955.fact: The **control** in a race to fall out of orbit. Its twin, Alchemy, unrolled a **70 m tape** to drag itself down fast; Augury had none, so engineers could compare how fast each fell.

48958.fact: A free-flying **satellite dispenser** with no engine of its own. It can release up to **16 customer satellites** one by one, watch each one go, and radio the results home.

51827.fact: One of **22 satellites** on a single Long March 8 rocket, a Chinese record at the time. It was also the first time that rocket flew **without side boosters**.

53448.fact: One of the small Jilin-1 Gaofen-03 imagers, which see details under **1 metre** across. The family’s prototype went up on China’s first **rocket launch from a ship** at sea.

54255.fact: Part of Jilin-1, China’s **largest commercial** satellite fleet, with about **130 satellites** in orbit by mid-2023. Its company later raised its goal to **300**.

55135.fact: One of **five** small satellites on a Ceres-1 rocket. Two were **Tianmu-1** weather satellites, which study the air by watching how **navigation signals** bend through it.

56963.fact: Made by **ICEYE**, a Finnish start-up from Aalto University that shrank **radar satellites** to a tiny size. It grew into the world’s largest radar satellite fleet.

58273.fact: Planet’s Doves aim to photograph **all of Earth’s land every day**. Their pictures help predict **crop harvests**, plan cities and respond to disasters.

58318.fact: Inside this small CubeSat is a telescope and a camera chip with a **colour filter pattern**, like the one in a phone camera. Planet calls these little satellites **Doves**.

58929.fact: Believed to be a small Russian **spy satellite** of about **150 kg**. Its design was reportedly inspired by American **SkySat** imagers, and its camera comes from a company in Belarus.

60203.fact: One of **eight** CubeSats on a Firefly Alpha rocket, including the University of Arizona’s CatSat with its **inflatable antenna**. Which one this object is hasn’t been confirmed.

60945.fact: Part of a mysterious set of Chinese **military test satellites**. Nine Yaogan-43s went up in August 2024, and this batch followed just **18 days** later.

61754.fact: A 6U **CubeSat** from Moscow’s Bauman university, built to study **space weather** and cosmic rays and to test a small **plasma thruster**.

61776.fact: One of a long series of **SITRO-AIS** CubeSats built by the Russian company SPUTNIX. Each listens for ships’ **position signals** to help keep shipping safe.

62385.fact: Came from **Bandwagon-2**, a SpaceX rideshare that carried South Korea’s **second radar satellite** for the 425 Project. Its 5-metre dish unfolds from **24 petals**.

62756.fact: Built by **SpaceX** using Starlink technology, under a programme called **Starshield**. It is believed to be part of a new US spy network made of many small satellites.

65269.fact: One of **four** satellites launched together on a small **Angara** rocket. They are believed to be Russian **spy cameras** weighing about 520 kg each.

67647.fact: This stage helped put **AlSat-3B**, an Algerian satellite, into orbit just **16 days** after its twin, AlSat-3A, rode the same kind of rocket. The Long March 2C first flew in 1982.

68373.fact: Built by **Bureau 1440**, a company named after the 1,440 orbits made by **Sputnik 1**. Rassvet means **dawn**, and this Russian internet fleet aims to start service in 2027.

69795.fact: Electra is named after a star in the **Pleiades**. It was one of six CubeSats from US schools and non-profits sent to the **space station** and released into orbit.

101031.fact: Carried **2,868 kg** of supplies to the space station, including new **roll-out solar panels** and an experiment growing **artificial retina** tissue for eyes.

1613.fact: One of the Air Force’s small **Orbiting Vehicle** test satellites. OV1-2 measured space radiation using detectors built to absorb it the same way **human tissue** does.

2122.fact: Carried **BORE**, the Background Optical Radiation Experiment: infrared sensors that measured the faint glow of the sky. It shared its rocket with its twin, **OV1-4**.

2401.fact: Navy navigation satellites like this were nicknamed **Oscars**, radio code for the letter O. This one lost power as its solar cell wiring wore out from **heating and cooling** in and out of sunlight.

2754.fact: Known to the Navy as **Oscar 12**, it was the first with a fix for failing solar cell wiring. From this one on, these navigation satellites lasted **over 14 years** on average.

15936.fact: Launched as a **stacked pair**, two Navy navigation satellites on one small Scout rocket. Spares like this were stored in orbit and switched on when they were needed.

19420.fact: When the Navy stopped using Transit for navigation in 1996, satellites like this kept on transmitting to help scientists study the **ionosphere**, the electrified layer of the upper air.

704.fact: Powered by a small **nuclear generator** instead of solar panels, it became the **first navigation satellite** put into regular use. Navy ships and submarines relied on it until late 1964.

2872.fact: **SURCAL** stands for surveillance calibration. Satellites like this gave the US Navy a known target to check and fine-tune its radar system for tracking objects in space.

3510.fact: A spinning Air Force weather satellite weighing just **175 pounds** (79 kg). Two tilted TV cameras let it photograph clouds around the **whole globe** for military forecasters.

4047.fact: From the Air Force’s **Block 4B** weather satellites. One spare from this series was never launched and was given to Chicago’s **Museum of Science and Industry** instead.

4363.fact: The first satellite of the US Army’s **map-making** command. Ground stations bounced radio signals off it to measure **exact positions on Earth**, which helps make accurate maps.

5435.fact: Collected readings from **weather balloons** floating high above Earth. A mistaken command from the ground once accidentally destroyed **71 of the balloons**.

6217.fact: Carried the **first germanium gamma-ray detector** ever flown on a satellite. To work properly it was kept chilled with frozen carbon dioxide, better known as **dry ice**.

6392.fact: Part of **Meteor-1**, the Soviet Union’s first series of weather satellites. Its TV camera photographed clouds in strips about **1,000 km wide**.

7574.fact: A heavy weather satellite of about **2,200 kg**, with two solar panels that turned to face the Sun. Along with a TV camera it carried an **infrared** camera that sensed the warmth of clouds.

8799.fact: One of 25 satellites launched under the **Meteor-1** name. The series was later replaced by the sharper-eyed **Meteor-2** weather satellites.

7924.fact: Shaped a bit like an **ocean buoy** and almost 3.7 m tall. It tested sending its data through another satellite, **ATS 6**, far above Earth, instead of straight to the ground.

11057.fact: Flew a stretched **12-hour orbit** reaching about 40,000 km out, so it lingered high over the far north. Molniya-3 satellites carried **civilian** phone and TV links.

15214.fact: A **Molniya-1T** that carried military communications for the Soviet network called **Korund**. Its long, looping orbit kept it high over the far north for hours at a time.

18946.fact: Its two dish antennas sat on **telescopic arms**, and each had its own little **optical tracker** so that one of them always stayed pointed at Earth.

11288.fact: Part of **Meteor-2**, the Soviet Union’s second generation of weather satellites. Besides cloud cameras it carried a sensor that measured **radiation** in space near Earth.

13000.fact: One of **six Soviet amateur radio satellites** launched together on a single rocket. RS-4 was an early experiment built by a **radio club**, so it had no relay for the public to use.

13492.fact: Japan’s test of **ion engines**, which push with a gentle stream of electrically charged mercury. Each engine pushed with only **2 millinewtons**, less than the weight of a paper clip.

14154.fact: Built from a **leftover Navy navigation satellite**, Transit-O 16. It studied ripples in the high-latitude sky that make radio signals **twinkle**, the way air makes stars twinkle.

16613.fact: France’s first **SPOT** Earth-imaging satellite, able to see details about **10 metres** across. It rode on the very last **Ariane 1** rocket.

20281.fact: A small **Czechoslovak** satellite that flew near the Soviet **Intercosmos 24** to study what happens when beams are fired into space. It had its own little gas-jet thruster.

21835.fact: Flew alongside **Intercosmos 25** in the APEX experiment, which fired beams of charged particles into space to try to create **artificial auroras**.

20441.fact: Built by students at **Weber State University**, this 16 kg ham radio satellite carried a **colour camera** that snapped pictures of Earth.

20547.fact: A small Navy test **radio relay** that rode on the very first **Pegasus** rocket, which was dropped from under the wing of a B-52 bomber before firing its engine.

20712.fact: Carried **24 canisters** of chemicals, which it released as clouds of metal vapour high above Earth so scientists could watch how space’s **magnetic fields** pushed them around.

21655.fact: A third-generation weather satellite with two TV camera systems and an infrared sensor called **Klimat**, the Russian word for ‘climate’.

22969.fact: Carried a NASA **ozone-mapping** instrument called TOMS, an American tool flying on a Russian weather satellite to keep watch on the **ozone layer**.

22489.fact: A **14 kg scout** for the Orbcomm messaging network. It listened around the world to how crowded the radio channels were before the full fleet of satellites was launched.

22783.fact: Relayed weather readings from about **50 ground stations** around the Mediterranean. Its unflown twin was later given to a Dutch university for **students** to learn on.

23233.fact: Like the rest of its block, it had a built-in rocket motor and acted as the **final stage of its own launch**. It then watched clouds for US military weather forecasters.

23463.fact: The only satellite in the Tsikada navigation series not given a **Kosmos** name. Tsikada satellites helped Soviet **merchant ships** work out where they were.

23710.fact: Canada’s first Earth-watching satellite used **radar**, so it could see through clouds and darkness. Its images helped ships find their way through **Arctic ice** for over 17 years.

23814.fact: Used **GPS** to know where it was and which way it was pointing. A 6 m pole with a weight on the end kept it standing upright, held by Earth’s **gravity**.

24883.fact: Its SeaWiFS camera read the **colour of the ocean** to map tiny floating plants called phytoplankton. It kept working for **13 years**, until 2010.

25024.fact: A **2,340 kg dummy satellite** for the second test flight of Europe’s Ariane 5. Sensors inside measured the **shaking** a real satellite would feel on the way up.

25503.fact: A **stand-in satellite** built in just **three months** for Ariane 5’s third test launch. It copied the weight and wobble of a TV satellite that wasn’t ready to fly.

25636.fact: The first small satellite made in **South Africa**, designed and built by engineering **students** at Stellenbosch University. It took pictures and relayed messages for ham radio users.

25757.fact: Between jobs it switched off and **tumbled freely** so the Sun warmed every side, a trick its builders called **barbecue mode**.

26064.fact: The **US Air Force Academy’s** first free-flying satellite, built by student cadets. Its batteries would not charge properly, so it lasted only **about a month**.

26621.fact: A tiny **6 kg** student-built cube from Sweden, with a mini camera to photograph **auroras** and sensors for the particles that make them glow.

27002.fact: Built to search the air and space above Earth for signals that might warn of **earthquakes** before they strike.

27368.fact: Carried a test copy of the **Hayabusa** asteroid probe’s return capsule. It most likely never separated from its carrier, and no contact was ever made.

27651.fact: Built to measure the total **sunlight** reaching Earth to within **0.01 percent**, to learn how small changes in the Sun affect our climate.

27470.fact: A Russian spy satellite with a **1.5 m telescope**, flying unusually high so it could watch targets for longer. It worked for about a year until its equipment section **lost air pressure**.

13912.fact: A **sun-studying** test satellite that got a free ride on an early Titan 3C rocket. A fault in the rocket’s top stage left it in a lower orbit than planned.

21263.fact: A NOAA weather satellite with its own built-in **rocket motor**, so it pushed itself into orbit as the last stage of the launch. The empty motor case stayed attached in space.

424.fact: Its two radio antennas stretched **45.7 m and 22.8 m** tip to tip. It bounced radio waves off the electrified upper air from above and kept working for **10 years**.

25394.fact: A Russian **Earth-watching** satellite that took colour pictures of the land in strips up to 600 km wide. Several small satellites from other countries hitched a ride on its rocket.

25977.fact: A **spy satellite** shared by France, Italy and Spain, able to see things about **1 metre** across. Its power system broke down in 2004, just short of its planned five years.

26547.fact: Built at La Sapienza University in Rome to test ordinary **off-the-shelf** parts, like regular batteries and solar panels, in space. It weighed only about **12 kg**.

28493.fact: A 15 kg Spanish test satellite. One of its jobs was to keep **communications** open with Spain’s research bases in **Antarctica**.

36605.fact: Flies just **a few hundred metres** from its twin, TerraSAR-X. Together the two radar satellites measured the height of **all of Earth’s land** for a 3D map called WorldDEM.

39241.fact: Part of the third of China’s satellite **triplets**, three craft launched together on one rocket. Experts believe the trios keep watch on **ships at sea**.

39765.fact: A secretive satellite that wasn’t announced at launch. Watchers saw it **manoeuvre** close to its own rocket’s upper stage, and it also carried a **ham radio** transmitter, RS-47.

40059.fact: NASA’s **carbon dioxide** tracker, built to measure the main gas behind climate change from space. It replaced the first OCO, lost when its **rocket failed** in 2009.

27858.fact: Built to study the chemistry of the **ozone layer**, especially over Canada and the Arctic, by looking at sunlight shining sideways through the air at each **sunrise and sunset**.

28051.fact: India’s **Resourcesat-1** carried three cameras, the sharpest able to see details about **5.8 metres** across, to help with farming, water and disaster planning.

28254.fact: Besides its main camera it carried a detector for **sprites**, rare red flashes of lightning above thunderstorms. It worked for over **12 years**.

28809.fact: Tested talking between satellites with **laser beams**, linking up with Europe’s ARTEMIS satellite far above. Planned to last one year, it kept going for **four**.

29499.fact: Europe’s first **polar-orbiting** weather satellite, a 4,244 kg giant. It measured temperature and moisture through the atmosphere, day and night, and relayed **rescue signals**.

31698.fact: A **radar** satellite that can see things about **1 metre** across, day or night and through clouds. It was Germany’s first satellite built as a partnership between government and a company.

32784.fact: A 6.5 kg Canadian nanosatellite built in just **seven months**. It picked up the radio beacons that ships broadcast, proving small satellites could **track ships** across the oceans.

33053.fact: Built to catch **gamma rays**, the most energetic kind of light. Its main telescope was about **50 times** more sensitive than the one flown before it.

33321.fact: **Huan Jing** means ‘environment’ in Chinese. HJ-1B carried an **infrared camera**, while its twin HJ-1A had a camera that split light into many colours.

33434.fact: **Chuangxin** means ‘innovation’. This 88 kg satellite worked like a **space post office**, picking up messages and delivering them later as it flew over the receiver.

37930.fact: A small **store-and-forward** messenger: it recorded data as it passed over one station and played it back over another. It shared its rocket with the test satellite **Shiyan 4**.

33499.fact: A **3 kg cube**, just 15 cm on a side, built by a Tokyo technical college to test **tiny thrusters** and take pictures of the land.

35681.fact: Part of the **Disaster Monitoring Constellation**, it photographed strips of Earth **600 km wide** to help after disasters. In 2021 it was renamed GEOSAT 1.

36036.fact: Built to measure how **wet the ground** is and how **salty the sea** is all over the world, two things that help shape weather and climate.

36415.fact: Part of China’s first satellite **triplet**, three craft launched together on one rocket. Experts believe the trio was built to keep watch on **ships at sea**.

37154.fact: A military **space mailbox**. It records messages as it passes over one station and delivers them when it reaches another, handy for **remote places** with no phone lines.

39058.fact: Launched with two siblings to carry military messages. Unlike them, this one **never manoeuvred** after launch and was reportedly considered a **complete loss**.

39483.fact: A military messenger satellite whose rocket carried a **secret passenger**, Kosmos 2491, that wasn’t announced at launch and later puzzled satellite watchers.

37212.fact: **Meridian** satellites took over from the famous Molniya fleet. They fly long, looping orbits that reach about **39,000 km** out to carry Russian communications.

37765.fact: Its purpose has **never been revealed**. Experts guess the Shijian 11 satellites might watch for **missile launches** or listen in on radio signals.

39624.fact: The sixth of China’s **mysterious** Shijian 11 satellites, which circle about 700 km up. China has never said what the series is for.

37794.fact: Ukraine’s Earth-imaging satellite, built for a five-year mission. It went silent in December 2012 when its **battery failed**, after about **one year**.

38753.fact: One of two **identical twin** probes sent through Earth’s dangerous **radiation belts**. Renamed the Van Allen Probes, both were switched off in 2019.

39092.fact: A 20 cm cube with a tiny telescope, built to watch the **brightest stars** for small changes in brightness at least **10 times** more precisely than from the ground.

39269.fact: A **10 cm metal ball filled with sand**. Radar tracks how fast air drag pulls it down, which tells scientists how thick the very **upper atmosphere** is.

39420.fact: A 3 kg Spanish CubeSat whose inside parts talked to each other with **light** instead of wires, testing a new way to build small satellites.

39444.fact: Built by **volunteer radio amateurs** for schools. Students could pick up its signals with a simple receiver and see live data from space on a computer.

40013.fact: Its camera can make out things **75 cm** across, and the whole satellite can tilt up to **45 degrees** sideways to photograph places off to the side of its path.

40022.fact: A 2 kg CubeSat from Taiwan’s National Cheng Kung University, born from an **online class** in 2003. It tested a tiny homemade **spinning wheel** for steering a satellite.

40042.fact: A **1 kg cube** built by students at Ukraine’s KPI technical university with help from Ukrainian **ham radio** fans. It tested a GPS and GLONASS navigation system.

40118.fact: Part of China’s **high-definition** Earth observation program. Its camera could pick out objects about **80 cm** across in strips 48 km wide.

40298.fact: Nicknamed **Sasuke**, it was built to prove that small, cheaper satellites could take sharp pictures of Earth. It sat finished for about **four years** waiting for a rocket.

40376.fact: Measured how much **water is in the soil** around the world, and whether the ground was frozen or thawed, to help forecast **floods and droughts**.

40908.fact: Built by **15 students** at Harbin Institute of Technology. It rode the very first Long March 6 rocket together with **19 other satellites**.

41173.fact: Nicknamed **Wukong**, it was built to search high-energy particles from space for clues to **dark matter**. Its particle-stopping block was the deepest of its kind ever flown.

41770.fact: Built in Europe for **Peru’s armed forces**, its camera can see things about **70 cm** across.

41786.fact: Unlike its twin, which was assembled in France, AlSat-2B was put together **in Algeria**, at a satellite centre in the city of **Oran**.

41888.fact: One of **eight** small NASA satellites built to measure winds inside **hurricanes** by catching GPS signals that bounce off the rough sea surface.

43585.fact: Officially a civilian imaging satellite, but experts believe it is really **military**. It was launched into an oval orbit that dipped to about **250 km**, lower than most satellites fly.

53876.fact: **Chuangxin** means ‘innovation’. CX-16B and its twin CX-16A were small Chinese Academy of Sciences satellites launched together on a **Kuaizhou-1A** rocket.

57047.fact: A Chinese test satellite for taking pictures from a **very low orbit**, where the camera is closer to the ground but thin air slowly drags on the spacecraft.

58992.fact: Built to sneak up on an old **Japanese rocket stage**, about 11 m long, and photograph it up close. It’s a first step toward clearing away **space junk**.

60209.fact: Carried experiments designed by students from a **middle school** and two high schools in Maine, including one to study **harmful algae blooms**.

22.fact: Carried the **first instrument** to measure Earth’s heat balance from space, built by Verner Suomi’s team. It showed that Earth soaks up **more sunlight** than scientists had thought.

162.fact: Credited with discovering **Hurricane Esther** in September 1961. One of its two TV cameras failed after **12 days**, but the other kept photographing tropical storms.

10664.fact: Took the **world’s first ultraviolet pictures** of the aurora from space. It kept working for more than **14 years**, until 1992.

735.fact: One of the first US **military weather satellites**, launched as a pair. Each time its spinning camera faced Earth, it could snap an area about **800 miles** (1,300 km) square.

1244.fact: Publicly called GGSE 2, it was really part of **POPPY 4**, a secret launch of satellites that listened for **Soviet radar** signals. The program stayed classified until 2005.

4259.fact: Part of **POPPY**, a secret US program that picked up signals from **Soviet radars** and warships. The program’s existence stayed classified until 2005.

1328.fact: Carried **laser reflectors**, so scientists could bounce laser light off it to track it precisely. It was switched off in 1973 because its radio clashed with more important spacecraft.

3093.fact: Carried **flashing lights** that cameras could photograph against the stars, plus laser reflectors, to help measure Earth’s exact shape. It flew a **retrograde** orbit, against Earth’s spin.

4793.fact: Its three fold-out solar panels were each over **4 m long** and covered with **3,420 solar cells**. It carried four cameras to photograph clouds for weather forecasters.

12553.fact: Besides watching clouds day and night, it collected readings from **free-floating balloons and ocean buoys** around the world and passed them on to scientists.

876.fact: A secret test of a Soviet **weather satellite**. It was the first of several prototypes that led to the Meteor weather satellites.

5846.fact: Part of **Tsiklon**, the Soviet Union’s first satellite navigation system. Navigators found their position by tracking how its radio signal changed **pitch** as it passed overhead.

7349.fact: A drum-shaped navigation satellite **3 m tall** and weighing about 800 kg. A long pole stuck out from it so **Earth’s gravity** would keep it pointing the right way.

9737.fact: The 23rd **Zaliv** navigation satellite. Its equipment rode inside a **sealed, pressurized** compartment filled with gas, instead of being open to space.

7003.fact: A joint **Soviet-French** mission to study the **northern lights** and the thin upper air near the poles. It carried on the work of Aureole 1, launched two years earlier.

17241.fact: Sent radio pulses down into the **ionosphere**, the electrified upper air. Its data showed aftershocks of the 1988 **Spitak earthquake** disturbing the air high above Earth.

18025.fact: Flew in a **triangle formation** with two partners. By timing when a ship’s radio or radar signal reached each one, the trio could work out **where the ship was**.

24293.fact: Russia’s **Auroral Probe** looped up to about **20,000 km** above the Northern Hemisphere. A small Czech-built partner satellite, Magion-5, flew with it.

26366.fact: A **dummy satellite** built to copy an Iridium phone satellite. It tested the new Briz-KM upper stage on the very first **Rokot-KM** launch.

27600.fact: Released two tiny **10 cm discs** in 2003, then tested a camera for tracking them. It was practice for future satellites that **inspect** other spacecraft up close.

28375.fact: Became one of the **most popular** ham radio satellites ever. It went silent in 2011 when its **batteries** began to fail.

28909.fact: The first upgraded **Gonets-M** satellite. **Gonets** means ‘messenger’: it stores messages and data and delivers them later to people in **remote places**.

29051.fact: One of **six** small satellites that studied the air by watching how **GPS signals** change as they pass through it. Their data helped improve **weather forecasts**.

30798.fact: One of five NASA probes that found what sets off sudden **brighter auroras**: magnetic fields in space snapping and reconnecting, about **96 seconds** before the lights flare.

31126.fact: Three tiny satellites named **Ralph, Gadget and Ted** were meant to unroll a **1 km tether** between them. Only a few metres came out, but Gadget stayed in touch for almost two months.

35868.fact: Built by **Moscow State University** to study flashes of light high above **thunderstorms**. In three months it recorded more than **1,000 flashes**.

38861.fact: Tested a new **heat-sensing camera** whose optics were kept chilled below **-20°C** by a tiny long-life cooler. It launched together with its partner, SJ-9A.

39197.fact: Launched on a rocket dropped from a **jet plane** over the Pacific. It studies the Sun’s lower atmosphere and has spotted **mini-tornadoes** and tadpole-shaped jets of gas.

39428.fact: A 3 kg Dutch CubeSat from **Delft University of Technology**, one of **32 satellites** on the same rocket. It tested new thruster and radio systems for future missions.

40073.fact: A **stand-in** for Canada’s M3M ship-tracking satellite. Canada pulled the real one from this Russian launch because of **sanctions** over the Ukraine crisis.

40715.fact: One of **three** identical satellites spaced evenly around the same orbit. Together they could photograph almost anywhere on Earth **once a day** in 1 m detail.

38354.fact: China launched it **without any announcement**, as it does for military missions. Officially it surveys land and crops, but experts believe it’s a **military** observer about 1,200 km up.

41473.fact: Thought to be a **spy camera** satellite. Later, groups of three small satellites also named Yaogan 30 were launched, reportedly to **work together** with it.

41853.fact: A small Aerospace Corporation CubeSat built to test a new kind of **electric thruster** for tiny satellites, plus wires and radiation shielding made of **carbon nanotubes**.

40961.fact: Part of the first launch of China’s commercial **Jilin-1** fleet: four satellites at once, including two that could shoot **high-definition colour video** of Earth.

41914.fact: A Chinese **video satellite**, built to film places on Earth in colour with detail of about **1.3 m**. It rode a small, quick-to-launch **Kuaizhou-1A** rocket.

44536.fact: One of five Zhuhai-1 satellites launched together. Four of them could split light into **256 colour bands** to study plants, water and crops, and one shot video.
