38013.fact: Hardware from a Soyuz launch from **French Guiana** that carried France’s Pléiades imaging satellite and **four ELISA** satellites built to pinpoint radar transmitters around the world.

63523.fact: A small satellite **released from China’s space station**. Independent tracking identifies it as **Naxing-4B**, carried to orbit in **2024**.

49319.fact: An unidentified object from the launch of **Xihe**, China’s first solar observatory in space. Xihe is named after a figure from Chinese legends about the **Sun**.

51828.fact: An unidentified object from a Long March 8 launch that carried **22 satellites** at once, the most ever lifted by a Long March rocket at the time.

54362.fact: From an Indian rocket that dropped off Oceansat-3, then fired new **orbit-changing thrusters** to sink lower and release **eight smaller satellites**.

55137.fact: An object from a small private **Ceres-1** rocket that carried five satellites, including two for **Tianmu-1**, a new fleet of weather satellites.

58280.fact: One of **36 SuperDoves** launched together by the company Planet. Its Dove satellites work as a team to photograph **Earth’s land every day**.

58322.fact: Planet’s Doves are tiny satellites about the size of a **loaf of bread**, 10 by 10 by 30 cm. This one flew up with **35 other Doves** on the same rocket.

61180.fact: An object from a **secret** Russian military launch on a light **Angara-1.2** rocket, which carried the classified satellites Kosmos 2577 and 2578.

61761.fact: An unidentified object from a Russian launch that carried two **space-weather** satellites and a record **53 small passengers**, the most ever on a Russian rocket.

61778.fact: One of **24 small ship-tracking satellites** packed onto a single Russian launch. It listens for the **radio beacons** that ships send out to say where they are.

62387.fact: An unidentified object from **Bandwagon-2**, a SpaceX rideshare carrying **30 payloads**, including **CroCube**, Croatia’s first satellite.

62405.fact: An unidentified object from SpaceX’s **Bandwagon-2** rideshare. Its 30 payloads included **Jackal MX-2**, a spacecraft built to fly itself around in orbit.

65270.fact: One of **four** secret Russian military satellites launched together on a light **Angara-1.2** rocket. The mission is classified but was listed as a **reconnaissance** launch.

67674.fact: One of **nine** Russian military satellites on one rocket. It was dropped off low, about **325 km** up, while the other eight went much higher, to about 500 km.

68826.fact: One of **four** Russian military satellites launched together. It circles only about **300 km** up, low for a satellite, and is listed as a military **imaging** satellite.

69796.fact: A small **payload released from the International Space Station**, still waiting for its real name. Objects let go from the station are listed under the station’s own **1998** launch.

29.fact: The **first successful weather satellite**. In about two and a half months it sent back some **23,000 pictures**, letting forecasters see whole storm systems from above for the first time.

202.fact: Partly powered by a small **nuclear battery**. In 1962 it was damaged by **Starfish Prime**, an American nuclear bomb test set off high above the Pacific.

705.fact: Rode piggyback with a Navy navigation satellite to study the space around its orbit. A new **all-electronic data switch** it tested worked perfectly and was copied on later satellites.

737.fact: In **June 2024**, more than 55 years after NASA stopped using it, astronomers caught a **brief radio blip** from it, probably a spark of static or a tiny space-rock hit.

897.fact: The **first Oscar**, the Navy’s production model of the Transit navigation satellite (Oscar is radio code for the letter O). It **stopped working after a few days**.

1271.fact: Launched with the secret **Poppy** spy satellites, which listened for **Soviet radar** signals. A Sun-watching science satellite on the same rocket served as the public cover story.

1420.fact: After the first Navy **Oscar** navigation satellites failed within days, Johns Hopkins engineers rebuilt this one. It lasted months, but poor factory workmanship still cut its life short.

1641.fact: Built to learn how dangerous the **Van Allen radiation belts** were for astronauts. Its rocket’s upper stage **exploded** in orbit, stranding it among the debris.

1864.fact: The first **Oscar** navigation satellite launched on a small **Scout rocket**. The Oscars before it rode bigger Thor rockets.

2125.fact: One of only three Block 2 **military weather satellites**, which added better **infrared sensors** to spot clouds by their warmth. One of its two sisters was lost at launch.

2418.fact: Unlike earlier military weather satellites, its two **tilted TV cameras** left no gaps at the equator, and it could beam images straight to small **army and ship terminals**.

2757.fact: Rolled along its orbit like a **cartwheel**, snapping cloud pictures each time its cameras faced Earth. It also measured how much sunlight and heat Earth **sends back to space**.

2873.fact: From the 1967 launch of **Poppy 5**, secret Navy satellites upgraded to catch radar signals from **Soviet anti-missile defences**.

3133.fact: The **first Oscar built by RCA**. RCA’s navigation satellites lasted so much longer than the expected 14 months that the Navy **stopped building new ones**.

3605.fact: A tiny satellite that hitched a ride on a **Corona spy camera** mission. Its kind reportedly carried a radio **mailbox for secret agents** using suitcase-sized radios.

4070.fact: A secret **Zaliv** satellite from Tsiklon, the first Soviet navigation system. Ships worked out where they were from how its radio tone **shifted in pitch** as it passed overhead.

4295.fact: Rode up on the 1969 launch that carried the Navy’s secret **Poppy** satellites, which listened from orbit for **Soviet radar** signals, along with several small test satellites.

4369.fact: Each **Zaliv** navigation satellite was a 3-metre drum of about 800 kg, with a long **boom** that let gravity keep it pointed the right way.

4799.fact: The seventh **Zaliv** navigation satellite and the last to fly at about 780 km. From the next launch on, the Soviets moved them **higher, to 1,000 km**.

5485.fact: Japan’s **first science satellite**. Its name means **“new star”**, and it carried receivers for radio waves from the Sun. An earlier try to launch it failed in 1970.

5903.fact: A secret **military weather satellite**. Its programme only got the public name Defense Meteorological Satellite Program in **December 1973**.

6822.fact: Released from a giant **Hexagon** spy satellite. It is thought to be one of the relay satellites that reportedly passed messages to **secret agents** on the ground.

6659.fact: From the **first Soviet weather satellite series**. Besides a TV camera it carried an **infrared camera** that mapped clouds by their heat.

7008.fact: A **Zaliv** navigation satellite from the first batch flown in steeper orbits. The system was later replaced by **Parus** for the military and **Tsikada** for civilians.

7363.fact: Although named Meteor, it was really the first **Meteor-Priroda**, a version that watched Earth’s land as well as the weather.

446.fact: Its name stands for **Army, Navy, NASA, Air Force**. It fired **bright flashes of light** so cameras could photograph it against the stars and measure the shape of Earth.

7615.fact: Sent pictures to ground stations on six continents. The very first to start receiving them, in April 1975, was in **Prince Albert, Saskatchewan**.

8026.fact: The **first Meteor-2**, the second generation of Soviet weather satellites. It carried three TV-style cameras plus a sensor that measured **radiation in space** near Earth.

8845.fact: Secretly a **Meteor-Priroda** Earth-watching satellite, and one of the first to test a Soviet **plasma thruster**, an engine that pushes with a stream of charged gas.

9841.fact: A test flight for Japan’s new **M-3H rocket**. It was only expected to work for about **two weeks**, long enough to try out steering with magnets and to measure ultraviolet light.

10674.fact: Replaced Ume 1, whose power failed after a month. It kept gathering data on the **radio-reflecting upper air** long after its planned 18-month mission, until 1983.

11060.fact: Was partly **its own rocket**: a solid motor built into the satellite fired to finish the climb to orbit. Its design was borrowed from a **military weather satellite**.

11416.fact: Besides watching clouds, it picked up signals from **drifting ocean buoys and weather balloons** around the world and passed their readings on to the ground.

12624.fact: Its wire antennas stretched **200 metres** from tip to tip. From high above the planet it took pictures of the **northern and southern lights** around the whole globe.

13001.fact: A Soviet **ham radio** satellite with a **robot operator**. Send it a Morse code call and it would answer with a short message and a contact number.

13718.fact: Meteor-2 weather satellites flew over both poles at about 850 to 950 km, so as Earth turned beneath them they could watch the clouds over the **whole planet**.

14452.fact: Flew on an **older Vostok-2M rocket**, even though the newer Tsiklon-3 had begun launching Meteor-2 weather satellites the year before.

15362.fact: An upgraded Navy **Transit** navigation satellite. Small **plasma thrusters** gave it gentle pushes to cancel the drag of the thin air at its height.

15952.fact: An **Oko** early-warning satellite that watched for the heat of **missile launches**. Early ones carried a **self-destruct** charge that fired if contact with the ground was lost.

16614.fact: **Sweden’s first satellite**. It reeled out four 40-metre wires to measure electric fields in the space where the **northern lights** are made.

17290.fact: A Soviet Meteor-2 weather satellite. Alongside its cloud cameras it carried **RMK-2**, an instrument that measured radiation in the space around Earth.

18123.fact: The first of its family to carry **SSM/I**, a microwave sensor. In July 2024 it **broke apart** in orbit, shedding at least five pieces of debris.

18960.fact: India’s **first home-built Earth-mapping satellite**. Its cameras could pick out things about 36 metres across, and it kept working for **8 years and 4 months**.

19467.fact: China’s **first weather satellite**, a test model. After just **39 days** its pointing system failed, so it could no longer aim its cameras properly.

20305.fact: From the **third generation** of Soviet Meteor weather satellites, which carried an infrared instrument named **Klimat**, Russian for climate.

20442.fact: Named after **LU**, the radio prefix used by Argentina’s ham radio stations. It stored messages from radio amateurs in its memory and **passed them on** later.

20607.fact: One of a pair of message-relay satellites. One MACSAT carried messages for troops in **Operation Desert Storm**, while the other’s long steadying boom never unfolded.

20788.fact: China’s second test weather satellite, launched with two **balloon satellites**. It worked until late 1992, when its pointing system failed.

21397.fact: Used a sideways-looking **radar** that sees through cloud and darkness. One Okean satellite could map the whole **Russian Arctic sea** in 3 to 5 days.

21688.fact: Improved on India’s IRS-1A with better **gyroscopes** to sense which way it pointed. It ended up working for **12 years and 4 months**, until December 2003.

22036.fact: The **first Gonets** prototype. Gonets means **“messenger”**, and the system was offered to send medical records to remote places that had no other links.

22490.fact: Collects readings from **automatic weather stations and ocean buoys** and relays them to Brazil. Built to last one year, it was **still working in 2011**.

22823.fact: Its cameras could see details **10 metres** across, and it carried a US instrument to measure **ozone** high above the poles. It stopped working in 1996 after a pointing failure.

22971.fact: A **university-built** satellite from TU Berlin, testing tiny **spinning wheels** for precise steering. Contact was lost after 39 days, but almost all its experiments were done.

23317.fact: Built by the **Yuzhnoye** design bureau in Ukraine. Its radar and microwave sensors watched **sea ice**, ocean temperature and water vapour, even through cloud.

23711.fact: Built with help from **60 college students**. It had **no batteries** and stayed bolted to its rocket’s upper stage, sending test signals for NASA’s new tracking dishes.

23827.fact: Looked both ways: cameras watched Earth’s land and **ocean colour**, while an Indian **X-ray telescope** on board studied flickering stars and other objects in deep space.

24305.fact: Mexico’s university satellite carried a small **radar** to catch the glowing trails of **meteors** as they burn up in the air. Its twin was lost when its rocket failed.

24920.fact: Built to catch **bursts of radio energy** from near Earth’s surface, as a way to check for **secret nuclear tests**. Its frame was made almost entirely of light carbon composite.

25025.fact: Rode the **second Ariane 5** with experiments from European universities. Its cameras **filmed the rocket’s nose cone opening** and the satellites separating.

25395.fact: A copy of FASat-Alfa, Chile’s first satellite, which **never separated** from the satellite it rode up with. Bravo carried an instrument to monitor the **ozone layer**.

25504.fact: Brazil’s second data-collection satellite. Its twin, SCD-2A, was **lost in 1997** on the first flight of Brazil’s own VLS-1 rocket.

25661.fact: Not a real satellite: a **4.5-tonne frame of pipes and plates** shaped like one. It tested the first Sea Launch rocket, fired from a **floating platform** on the equator.

25758.fact: India’s first satellite built mainly to study the **oceans**. Its colour camera tracked **plankton blooms**, and a microwave sensor measured sea temperature and wind.

25978.fact: A small **French military** satellite built to **listen for radio signals** from chosen regions of the world.

26065.fact: Built by students at **Arizona State University**. A ham radio operator in **South Africa** heard it 50 minutes after launch, but a power fault silenced it after just 14 hours.

26374.fact: A military test satellite that carried an experiment in **laser communications** between spacecraft, plus an **infrared camera** for spotting aircraft in flight.

26548.fact: **Malaysia’s first microsatellite**, built in Britain with Malaysian engineers learning on the job. It sent back its **first pictures of Earth** within a week of launch.

26898.fact: Covered in **126 corner-cube mirrors** that bounce laser beams straight back, so ground stations could measure its distance precisely. It first checked the path of Japan’s new H-2A rocket.

27003.fact: A follow-up to Pakistan’s first satellite, designed and built mostly in Pakistan. A British-made camera watched **clouds**, and other sensors measured **radiation from the Sun**.

27386.fact: The **largest civilian Earth-watching satellite** ever built. Contact was lost in April 2012, and the dead giant may take about **150 years** to fall back.

27534.fact: Its name means **hope** in Russian. Along with its navigation job, it carried a new **search-and-rescue** receiver for picking up distress beacons.

27605.fact: Built privately by German companies. It tested a tiny experimental **thruster** that spun it faster, and sent data home through another company’s satellite network, **Orbcomm**.

27664.fact: A 28 kg robot inspector. After launch it **flew circles around its own rocket stage** on its own, sending live video to the ground, a first test of satellites checking up on others.

27939.fact: A **training satellite** for Russian military academy cadets, built on a leftover body from an old communications satellite. It also tested parts for future **GLONASS** navigation satellites.

28054.fact: The first military weather satellite to carry **SSMIS**, a sensor that reads microwaves coming from the air and sea. It was also one of the last to fire its **own built-in rocket motor** to reach orbit.

28366.fact: Launched under the name **LatinSat D**. It belongs to a planned network of small satellites for **tracking** equipment and vehicles on the move anywhere on Earth.

28376.fact: Built to study the **chemistry of the air**, from the ground up to the edge of space, including the **ozone layer**. Three were planned, but only this one was built.

28498.fact: Studied clouds and tiny floating particles by checking how **polarized** the sunlight bouncing off them was, the same effect that polarized sunglasses use.

28810.fact: Its name means **“dawn”** in Japanese. This small satellite took close-up looks at the **fine structure of the northern lights**.

28931.fact: Unrolled a **22-metre** solar panel while six onboard cameras watched. It mapped Earth by camera and radar until it suddenly **lost all power** in April 2011.

29052.fact: Measured how **GPS signals bend** as they pass through the air, to help weather forecasts. In 2007 it lost **half its power** but kept sending data at some angles to the Sun.

29505.fact: Flew as one of a **pair** of Chinese satellites studying radiation in space. Some experts suspect the pairs also tested **radio-listening spy** equipment.

31113.fact: Haiyang means **ocean** in Chinese. Its colour scanner measured **plankton** and sediment in the sea, as well as water temperature along China’s coasts.

31127.fact: A **12 kg** Saudi communications satellite that stored messages and **delivered them later** as it passed over the right spot. It was built at a Saudi research institute.

31797.fact: Lupe is German for **magnifying glass**. Part of Germany’s first military satellites, its radar was tested on the ground by taking pictures of the **Space Station** passing overhead.

32785.fact: A tiny Tokyo Tech satellite whose brain was a **handheld organizer** (PDA) made by Hitachi. Built for a **two-month** mission, it was still sending data years later.

33105.fact: Measured the **height of the sea** to within a few centimetres, covering 95% of the ice-free ocean every 10 days. That shows how sea level and currents are changing.

33331.fact: At launch it was the **sharpest commercial camera in orbit**, seeing details 41 cm across. **Google’s logo** was painted on its rocket, since Google used its pictures for maps.

33446.fact: Its name simply means **“remote sensing”**. Officially it watches Earth for the government, but it is likely also used as a **military spy camera**.

33504.fact: Studied **solar flares** with 12 instruments, including X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes from **India**. It flew on the very **last Tsiklon-3 rocket**.

35682.fact: Its pictures tracked the building of Dubai’s **Palm Islands**, and the United Nations used them to guide relief after the **2011 tsunami** in Japan.

35869.fact: Built by students at **Ufa State Aviation Technical University**. Its camera could spot features 50 metres across, to help watch over **forests and water**.

36037.fact: A small ESA test satellite that watched the Sun with **LYRA**, a light meter made with **diamond** sensors, and a camera that saw the Sun in ultraviolet.

36508.fact: Built to measure how **thick the sea ice** is near the North Pole. It replaced CryoSat-1, **lost in a rocket failure** in 2005, and reaches closer to the pole than earlier missions.

39630.fact: Lost in **February 2016** after a power failure cut off its controls. Its replacement was already built, but Congress had it **scrapped** to save storage costs.

36795.fact: Could lean up to **26 degrees** forwards, backwards or sideways to photograph places it wasn’t directly over, so it could check the same spot more often.

37165.fact: Like other Yaogan spy satellites, it also has a secret military name in the **Jianbing** family, which means **“vanguard”** or “point soldier”.

37214.fact: An early test model of China’s **second generation** of polar weather satellites. It carried about a dozen instruments, including two that measured the **ozone layer**.

37781.fact: Watched the sea with **microwave instruments** that work through cloud, measuring the height of the sea surface, ocean **winds** and water temperature.

37795.fact: A box of experimental **navigation electronics** that never left its rocket. It stayed bolted to the spent upper stage and ran on the rocket’s own batteries for a short test.

37931.fact: Shiyan means **“experiment”**. This Chinese test satellite carried a digital camera system able to make **3D maps** of the land below.

38038.fact: Ziyuan means **resources**. A Chinese-only cousin of the China-Brazil satellites, its sharpest camera could see things about **2.4 metres** across, for mapping land and disasters.

38358.fact: The first space telescope to take sharp pictures in **high-energy X-rays**. After launch it unfolded a **10-metre mast** to hold its mirrors far enough from its cameras.

38755.fact: Took pictures sharp enough to see objects **2 metres** across, in squares 60 km wide. Its twin, SPOT 7, was later **sold to Azerbaijan** and renamed Azersky.

38995.fact: Flies a long, stretched **Molniya orbit** that swings out to about 39,000 km, so it spends most of each lap in view of the **Arctic**, which normal communications satellites serve poorly.

39059.fact: A Russian military **mailbox** satellite, launched as a trio. One of its two sisters **never moved** after launch and was reportedly written off as a complete loss.

39133.fact: Aist means **stork** in Russian. Built by Samara university students and scientists, it measured Earth’s **magnetic field** and hits from tiny bits of space dust and debris.

39202.fact: China has never said what the Shijian-11 satellites are for. Experts guess they could **watch for missile launches** or **listen to radio signals**.

39249.fact: Gonets means **“messenger”**. It works like a flying post office: it **stores messages** as it passes one place and drops them off when it passes another.

39270.fact: A **10 cm metal ball filled with sand**. Radars tracked how fast air drag pulled it down, showing how the upper atmosphere **thickens** when the Sun is stormy.

39421.fact: An Italian university satellite carrying a **biology experiment** on how weightlessness and radiation affect **brain tumour cells**.

39429.fact: A shoebox-sized **5.2 kg** camera satellite, one of the very first test **Doves** from the young start-up then called Cosmogia, now known as Planet.

39445.fact: A **10 cm cube** satellite built by students in **Narvik**, Norway, to photograph Earth and measure its own temperature. Sadly it never worked once it reached orbit.

39484.fact: A modern Russian **mailbox** satellite in the Strela family. A retired Austrian colonel convicted of spying for Russia had been trained to send messages via **Strela-3** satellites.

40920.fact: Strela means **“arrow”**. These satellites grab messages as they pass over a sender and **beam them down later** when they reach the receiver, handy in remote regions.

40061.fact: A civilian cousin of Russia’s military **Strela** satellites. The Gonets system was first offered for sending **medical records** to remote places.

40310.fact: Its orbit suggests it belongs to the same family as Yaogan 4 and 11, but some think it marks the start of an **improved version** of these likely military cameras.

39766.fact: Unlike the first ALOS, it has **no cameras at all**, only an upgraded **radar** that sees through cloud and darkness and can look to either side to check on disasters.

40014.fact: Nicknamed **Tita**, this Argentine test satellite runs the free computer system **Debian Linux**. It tried out parts for a later fleet of small Earth-watching satellites.

40043.fact: Built by **Iraqi students** at a university in Rome, it had a camera with special software to spot **dust storms** over Iraq, sending pictures to Rome and Baghdad.

40074.fact: The UK Space Agency’s first **pilot CubeSat**. It also carried **FUNcube-2**, a radio project to get schoolkids excited about space, electronics and physics.

40119.fact: Part of a tiny six-satellite **star-watching** team from Canada, Austria and Poland. It watched stars in **red light** while its Polish twin Lem watched in blue.

40536.fact: South Korea’s first satellite with an **infrared camera** that senses heat, so it can take pictures **at night**. Its regular camera sees details about 55 cm across.

40716.fact: A small British satellite that can see objects about **1 metre** across. Flying as a team of three, the satellites could revisit the same place **every day**.

40969.fact: The **first satellite** designed, built and run by students at the **University of Alaska Fairbanks**.

41240.fact: Measured the height of the sea surface to within about **4 cm**. It flew just **1 minute behind** Jason-2 at first, so no ocean data was missed between the two.

41556.fact: Has **three cameras**: one looking straight down, one tilted forwards and one backwards. Combining their views makes **3D maps** of the land.

41771.fact: Besides photos, SkySats can film **video clips up to 90 seconds** long from space. Google bought the company that built them for **$500 million** in 2014.

41787.fact: A test model for BlackSky’s fleet of sharp-eyed small satellites. It met **every goal**, so its backup twin, Pathfinder 2, **never needed to launch**.

41857.fact: A Chinese satellite for watching weather, the sea and space conditions. Its sister, Yunhai-1 02, **broke apart** in orbit in March 2021.

41890.fact: Built to measure **hurricane winds** by catching GPS signals that bounce off the rough sea. With its solar panels unfolded, it is about the size of a **swan**.

41948.fact: Its camera sees details **60 cm** across and can shoot a minute of video of one spot. Its rocket also carried **103 other satellites** from seven countries.

40024.fact: **Brazil’s first CubeSat**, a 10 cm cube built with university students in Santa Maria. It measured Earth’s **magnetic field** over the South Atlantic Anomaly, a weak spot in that field.

43758.fact: A shoebox-sized satellite built largely by **university students** in Colorado to measure **X-rays from the Sun**, which flare up during solar storms. Its twin flew in 2016.

44538.fact: Carries a **hyperspectral camera** that splits light into many very narrow colours, about 2.5 nanometres apart, to tell crops, water and minerals apart from space.

48907.fact: A DARPA test of **laser links** that let satellites talk to each other. It was built in just **nine months**, then damaged before launch when its release mechanism fired by accident.

49469.fact: A sharp-eyed BlackSky camera satellite with a 24 cm telescope that can see things about **1 metre** across. Each one can take up to **1,000 pictures a day**.

51843.fact: An unidentified object from the second flight of China’s **Long March 8** rocket, which carried **22 satellites** into orbit at once.

53754.fact: A **space tug** designed to ferry small satellites to their orbits. Its engines burn **hydrogen peroxide and rubbing alcohol**, a greener fuel. This flight carried a Boeing radio test.

55010.fact: **Catalonia’s first** Earth-watching satellite. Its camera can see things about **5 metres** across and was meant to track the effects of **climate change** on the region.

55861.fact: Shiyan means **“experiment”**. China has released **no details at all** about what this secretive satellite does.

57206.fact: An unidentified object from a 2023 Russian launch that carried a **Meteor-M weather satellite** along with dozens of small student and research satellites.

58282.fact: A **SuperDove**: a shoebox-sized satellite whose camera sees **eight colours** of light, including yellow and “red edge”, useful for spotting things like **algal blooms** in water.

58328.fact: Flying in a big flock, SuperDoves like this one can photograph places **almost every day**, with each pixel covering about **3 metres** of ground.

59112.fact: A Würzburg university satellite that tested **artificial intelligence** in orbit. It **trained its own AI** on board to spot unusual things on Earth’s surface.

60246.fact: A student-built satellite with an antenna shaped like a **beach ball**, inflated with gas once in space. It carried enough gas to **refill it 25 times** in case of leaks.

61229.fact: An unidentified object from a 2024 Chinese launch whose only satellite, Jitianxing A-01, carried a camera for Earth plus a **selfie camera** to look at itself.

61763.fact: A 3.2 kg student satellite from a St. Petersburg telecom university. It tested **LoRa**, a low-power radio used for **smart devices**, and took pictures of Earth.

61780.fact: A shoebox-sized Russian satellite that listens for **AIS**, the automatic radio beacons that ships broadcast, to help keep track of vessels and make sailing **safer**.

62391.fact: Built by **Czech high school students**, whose idea won NASA’s Conrad Challenge. It is a target for ground **lasers** being tested to fix broken satellites and deal with space junk.

62617.fact: SCOT stands for **Space Camera for Object Tracking**. Billed as the first commercial space-surveillance satellite, it can track objects as small as **5 cm**.

62850.fact: Meant to join India’s **NavIC** navigation system, but the valves feeding its thrusters **failed to open**, leaving it stuck in a long, looping orbit far from its spot.

67683.fact: A Thai student-built CubeSat that can carry up to **10 small experiments**. Japan’s deployer on the **International Space Station** pushed it into space on 3 February 2026.

68827.fact: One of four secret Russian military satellites launched together. Experts believe they may be small **spy cameras**, but Russia has not said what they do.

23464.fact: Its instruments were named after characters in **Astrid Lindgren’s** books, like **PIPPI** and EMIL. The whole satellite was built in a year for about **1.4 million US dollars**.

45.fact: It shared its rocket with a secret passenger: **GRAB 1**, the first successful American spy satellite, hidden behind a cover story about studying the Sun.

205.fact: Carried the **first poem ever sent into orbit**, written by a Yale professor and engraved on its instrument panel. A 1962 nuclear test in space later ruined its solar cells.

503.fact: Sent the **first American TV pictures across the Pacific**. The first broadcast to Japan, in November 1963, ended up carrying news of **President Kennedy’s assassination**.

716.fact: The first satellite with **Automatic Picture Transmission**: any weather station with a simple receiver could download live cloud pictures as it passed overhead.

746.fact: Launched together with its twin **Elektron 2**, the **first time the Soviet Union put two satellites up on one rocket**. Its orbit kept it inside Earth’s radiation belts.

899.fact: Covered in **360 small glass mirrors** so scientists could bounce **laser beams** off it from the ground and measure its orbit very precisely.

1430.fact: The **tenth and last** of the original TIROS weather satellites. Its two TV cameras photographed clouds over the whole sunlit side of Earth.

1726.fact: Built to **measure the shape of Earth**. It fired **flashing xenon lights** that cameras on the ground photographed against the stars to pin down exact positions.

1952.fact: A Navy **Transit-O** navigation satellite, also called “Oscar”. Ships used the Transit system to find their way until GPS replaced it at the end of **1996**.

2142.fact: Meant to be NASA’s first big **space telescope**, but a **power failure** ended the mission after **three days**, before its instruments were ever switched on.

2435.fact: One of its first pictures showed **Hurricane Inez**, a powerful storm, over the Bahamas and Florida. Its last camera kept working for **two years**.

2874.fact: Part of **Poppy**, a secret US Navy spy programme that recorded **Soviet radar signals** from orbit. Its existence was only revealed in **2005**.

3173.fact: Mapped the **Van Allen radiation belts** as high as 8,000 km and caught electrons getting stronger during a **solar storm** in June 1968.

3615.fact: Worked for over **seven years**. On **Christmas Day 1974** it photographed **Cyclone Tracy**, the storm that flattened the Australian city of Darwin.

4132.fact: A metal **cone** only 66 cm long. The Air Force used its known shape to **calibrate radars** that identify objects in space.

4138.fact: Part of **Tsiklon**, the **first Soviet satellite navigation system**. The project began in the 1950s but delays meant it only started working in **1972**.

4382.fact: Weighed **173 kg**, more than the first satellites of the four earlier space nations **put together**. A shiny skirt on its rocket’s last stage was meant to help people see it.

4952.fact: Its name, **Tansei**, means “light blue”, the school colour of the University of Tokyo, which built it. It was **Japan’s second satellite**.

6235.fact: The first working weather satellite with **no TV cameras**. It made cloud pictures with **radiometers**, sensors that scan heat and light line by line.

7646.fact: A ball just **24 cm wide** with a heavy uranium core and 60 mirrors. Lasers bounced off it helped scientists map the world’s **ocean tides**.

1272.fact: A 26 cm ball sprouting **12 rods, each 7.6 metres long**, like a giant porcupine. Radars on the ground used it as a big, known target to **calibrate** themselves.

5557.fact: Launched in secret as **DSAP-5B**, a military weather satellite. The Air Force only gave the series its public name, **DMSP**, in December 1973.

7411.fact: The **first Block 5C** satellite, the eighth version of the US military’s polar-orbiting weather satellites. It was built by **RCA Astro**.

13736.fact: A Block 5D-2 military weather satellite built to act as the **last stage of its own rocket**, firing its own motor to finish the climb into orbit.

14506.fact: Part of a US military weather programme so secret it was only **made public in 1973**. Its infrared sensors let forecasters see clouds **at night**.

8195.fact: A Molniya-2: only **17** were launched before newer models replaced them. They carried programmes for the Soviet **Orbita TV network**.

17328.fact: One of **53 Molniya-3** relay satellites. They started out carrying civilian phone calls and TV, and from the 1980s also served the **military**.

21706.fact: **Molniya** is Russian for **“lightning”**: the name comes from how fast these satellites race through the lowest point of their orbit.

8860.fact: Nicknamed **Wideband**, it beamed radio signals down through the upper atmosphere to learn how **disturbed plasma** scrambles radar and radio links.

5917.fact: A **2,200 kg** weather satellite with two eyes: a TV camera for clouds in daylight and an **infrared camera** that saw clouds by their warmth.

9903.fact: One of four Meteor satellites used to test **plasma thrusters**, engines that push with electrified gas. It flew the smaller **SPD-50** model.

11605.fact: It has **broken apart several times**, leaving 83 known pieces of debris. Sixty of them were still circling Earth in 2019.

16735.fact: A second-generation Meteor weighing **1,300 kg**. Three TV-style scanners photographed clouds in visible and **infrared light**.

20826.fact: One of **21 Meteor-2** weather satellites launched between 1975 and 1993. Besides clouds, they measured **radiation** in the space around Earth.

6707.fact: A **Zaliv** navigation satellite. Soviet **nuclear submarines** used satellites like it to fix their position so they could aim their missiles more accurately.

7094.fact: Secretly the **16th Zaliv** navigation satellite. Its public name, Kosmos 628, gave **nothing away** about what it really did.

10702.fact: Carried a **heat-sensing band** that could have mapped Earth at night, but it **failed** four months after launch. The rest of the satellite worked for five years.

11080.fact: Its **TOMS** instrument recorded the **Antarctic ozone hole**, but its software set the odd readings aside. British scientists reported the hole first.

12645.fact: Better known as **Bulgaria 1300**, named for the 1300th birthday of the Bulgarian state. It was **Bulgaria’s first satellite**.

13002.fact: One of **six amateur radio satellites** launched together on one rocket. Their bodies were based on Soviet **military relay satellites**.

15427.fact: Carried **ERBE**, an experiment that measured the energy flowing between Earth and space, plus a sensor that mapped the **ozone layer** worldwide.

16181.fact: The **first successful flight** of the Zenit-2 rocket, after two failures earlier in 1985. It carried a **stand-in** for a Tselina-2 spy satellite.

18214.fact: An **Okean** ocean watcher. Its sideways-looking radar and microwave sensors tracked **sea ice** and ocean temperature across the **Russian Arctic**.

19070.fact: Launched **stacked on top of a twin**, Oscar 32, so the Navy could keep spare Transit navigation satellites waiting in orbit until needed.

19531.fact: Built to last **2 years**, it worked for almost **16**. It also listened for **emergency beacons** to help search-and-rescue teams.

20322.fact: Showed that the **Big Bang’s afterglow** matches theory perfectly and found its faint ripples. Two of its scientists won the **2006 Nobel Prize** in Physics.

20465.fact: A secret **Tselina-R**, one of only four. It carried an experimental payload built to **listen in on communication links**.

21422.fact: The third of four **Tselina-R** spy satellites. It weighed about **2,000 kg** but was only built to last around **six months**.

20608.fact: Launched as a pair with MACSAT 1 to test **store-and-forward** messaging. One of the two relayed messages for troops during **Operation Desert Storm**.

22038.fact: Secretly **Gonets #2**, an early test of a civilian message-relay system built from the Soviet military **Strela-3** satellites.

22561.fact: The **first flight** of the Start-1 rocket, built from a **Topol nuclear missile**. It carried a dummy test load called EKA-1.

22824.fact: Twin of the French satellite **Starlette**, sent up to cover the parts of Earth its sister missed. A dense 24 cm ball with **60 laser mirrors**.

23323.fact: Designed, built and tested in just **18 months**. The “P” in its name means it was made to ride India’s new **PSLV** rocket.

23715.fact: Its 60 cm mirror was chilled to just **1.7 degrees above absolute zero** with superfluid helium, making it 1,000 times more sensitive than the **infrared** telescope before it.

23851.fact: In 1997 a scrap of the rocket that launched it fell back and **tapped a woman on the shoulder** in a park in Tulsa, Oklahoma. She was unhurt.

24720.fact: Unfolded an **8-metre dish** in orbit and linked up with radio telescopes on the ground to work as **one telescope wider than Earth**. It was the first mission built to do it.

25068.fact: Built to study Earth’s **magnetic bubble** near the equator. A computer failure ended the mission after **five months** instead of the planned two years.

25509.fact: Built by **students** in Alabama so radio amateurs worldwide could request pictures from it, but no one ever managed to send it commands, so **no photos came back**.

25682.fact: In 2003 a pair of tiny mirrors in its camera broke, leaving **zig-zag gaps** that miss about **22%** of each picture. It kept taking pictures until 2024 and was switched off in 2025.

25789.fact: Measured **winds over the ocean** by bouncing radar off tiny waves. Planned for 3 years, it gathered over **400,000 wind readings a day** for a decade.

26091.fact: One of the tiny **Picosats** released from the student-built satellite **OPAL**, each weighing a few hundred grams. Two of them were even tied together by a wire.

26930.fact: Despite its name, a **67 kg** satellite that tested electronics in space. **PICO** is made from the first letters of its four experiments.

26384.fact: **Nadezhda** means “hope” in Russian, a good name for a satellite that listened for distress beacons. Each one weighed **870 kg**.

25396.fact: **Thailand’s first** microsatellite, built by Thai engineers working with Surrey Satellite Technology in England. It was later renamed **Thai-Paht**.

26549.fact: One of the **first Saudi Arabian** satellites, a **10 kg** box built in Riyadh to collect messages and pass them on later, like a flying post office.

27607.fact: Carries an **FM radio repeater** that radio amateurs anywhere in the world can use to chat through space, whenever its batteries allow.

27004.fact: A **47 kg** team effort: **Morocco** made the payload and a Berlin university built the body. Its other name is **Zarkae Al Yamama**.

27559.fact: **Algeria’s first satellite** and the first launched of the **Disaster Monitoring Constellation**. Built to last 5 years, it worked for almost 8.

27783.fact: Studied the sky in **ultraviolet light** to trace how galaxies made their stars. It used the **first** ultraviolet beam-splitter ever flown in space.

28057.fact: Its wide camera covered a strip **890 km** across, enough to see the whole of Earth about every **five days**.

28368.fact: Its name stands for **Detection of Electromagnetic Emissions Transmitted from Earthquake Regions**. It hunted for radio signals that might warn of **earthquakes**.

28382.fact: Part of Double Star, the **first Chinese satellites to carry European science instruments**. It teamed up with ESA’s Cluster satellites to study what makes **aurorae**.

28523.fact: Built by **scholars and students** of Moscow State University to celebrate its **250th birthday**. It weighed only about 30 kg.

28890.fact: Its sharpest camera saw details **4 metres** across. It beamed pictures straight down to Beijing for maps, farming and **disaster monitoring** across China.

28980.fact: Flew a tiny, odd-looking antenna that was **designed by a computer** using artificial evolution, one of ten new technologies tested on this mission.

29506.fact: Flew as a **pair** with SJ-6 02A. Officially it studied space radiation, but it may also have tested **electronic eavesdropping** gear.

31117.fact: **Egypt’s first** Earth-watching satellite, built together with Ukrainian engineers so Egypt could learn the skills itself. Contact was **lost in 2010**.

31128.fact: **Colombia’s first satellite**, a tiny CubeSat built by university students. Its name means **“Freedom”**. Expected to last 50 days, it was still working two years later.

32060.fact: Its camera sees details just **half a metre** across. A US intelligence agency helped pay for it, and some of its pictures are **kept private**.

32786.fact: The **first satellite** built on India’s small IMS design. It shared its rocket with **nine others**, including eight tiny research satellites from five countries.

33312.fact: The company behind it got early money from a German **farm insurance firm**. Planet, which bought the five-satellite fleet, retired it in **2020**.

33393.fact: A 1.5 m **aluminium dummy** that stayed bolted to its rocket. It rode SpaceX’s Falcon 1, the **first privately built liquid-fuel rocket to reach orbit**, after three failures.

33492.fact: The world’s **first satellite built just to watch greenhouse gases**. It measures carbon dioxide and methane at **56,000 places** around the planet.

33591.fact: In 2003 it **fell to the factory floor** when bolts were missing from its cart. Repairs cost **$135 million**, and it later flew as the last of its line.

35683.fact: Also called **Blue Peter 1**: children watched it being built and launched on TV. It was part of the **Disaster Monitoring Constellation**.

35871.fact: A ball of **layered glass** built to reflect laser beams back to Earth for precise tracking. Its name means **Ball Lens In The Space**. A collision with debris ended its useful tracking mission in 2013.

36588.fact: Tested whether cheap, **off-the-shelf** parts, the kind made for ordinary electronics, could survive in space. It carried **nine experiments**.

36796.fact: **India’s first picosatellite**, dreamed up by four students who met at a space conference. In the end about **45 students** worked on it.

37216.fact: **COSMO-SkyMed** stands for Constellation of small Satellites for the **Mediterranean** basin Observation. It is one of four identical Italian radar satellites.

37818.fact: A Navy test satellite offering **10 radio channels** to troops. Its stretched orbit climbs to **12,050 km**, giving about two hours of talk time per orbit.

38007.fact: One of four French spy **microsatellites** flying just a few kilometres apart to record **radar and radio** signals, testing ideas for a future system called CERES.

38248.fact: When launched, the **heaviest** Earth-watching satellite India had ever sent up. Its radar pictures helped estimate **rice harvests** for India’s food planning.

39084.fact: Launched as the **Landsat Data Continuity Mission** and renamed once it started work. It captures over **700 scenes a day**, almost three times as many as Landsat 7.

39150.fact: The **first of the Gaofen** series, China’s civilian high-resolution Earth-watching fleet. It shared its rocket with small satellites from **Turkey, Argentina and Ecuador**.

39250.fact: **Gonets** means **“messenger”** in Russian. The system started as a government project and was handed to a **private company** in 1996.

40062.fact: One of the **Gonets** message-relay satellites. Three earlier Gonets satellites were **lost** when their rocket failed in December 2000.

40552.fact: The Gonets system began in **1992** with two test satellites. Modernised models like this one were launched to **replace** the original fleet.

39485.fact: Works like a **mailbox in space**: it stores encrypted messages and passes them on later. Rodnik is the newest version of the Soviet **Strela** (“Arrow”) design.

40921.fact: A Rodnik, the newest kind of Strela relay satellite. A retired Austrian colonel who spied for Russia had been trained to pass secret messages through **Strela-3** satellites.

39634.fact: In August 2016 a **millimetre-sized particle** smashed into one of its solar panels. Onboard cameras showed the damage, but the satellite kept working.

40336.fact: Built to replace **CBERS-3**, which was lost when its rocket failed in 2013. China and Brazil each paid **$125 million** for it.

41335.fact: The **first of four** Sentinel-3 ocean satellites. Its launch slipped by months, partly because the **launch pad had to be recertified** while it was being fuelled.

41579.fact: A Russian military **mapping** satellite. Geo-IK-2 satellites help make very precise **3D maps** of Earth and track the slow drift of **tectonic plates**.

41772.fact: Can film **video clips up to 90 seconds** long from orbit, sharp enough to watch cars and shipping containers. Google once owned the fleet.

41875.fact: Turkey’s sharp-eyed military satellite, seeing details under **1 metre** across. In 2025 its **100,000th photo** showed the Çanakkale Martyrs’ Memorial.

41891.fact: One of **eight** small satellites dropped from a rocket launched off an **aeroplane**. They read GPS signals bouncing off the sea to measure **winds inside hurricanes**.

42063.fact: Flies on the **opposite side of Earth** from its twin, Sentinel-2A, so together they can photograph the same place every **5 days** instead of 10.

22979.fact: Renamed **Myojo** after launch. It stayed **attached to its rocket** on purpose to check how accurately Japan’s brand-new H-II rocket reached orbit.

23465.fact: A **115 kg** test for a planned network relaying stored messages to remote users. Its links never worked well enough, and it was **switched off in 1996**.

24925.fact: A **pretend Iridium satellite**: one of two mass models launched to test a new version of China’s Long March rocket and the device that releases satellites.

25991.fact: The first **Block 5D-3** satellite, the eleventh version of the US military’s polar weather satellites. It needed an extra **kick motor** to reach its orbit.

27421.fact: Its **HRS** camera looked forwards and backwards at the same time, taking **3D pictures** that measured the height of the land to within about 10 to 15 metres.

27940.fact: A small box **bolted to its rocket’s upper stage**. It **emailed** reports on the rocket’s shaking and position down to Earth through Orbcomm satellites.

29092.fact: One of China’s **first radar imaging satellites**. Almost four years after launch it **broke apart**, probably from an explosion inside it.

39011.fact: The lead satellite of a **trio** launched together. They are reported to keep watch on **ships at sea**, much like the US Navy’s NOSS spy satellites.

41026.fact: One of only two **Jianbing-11** class satellites, each launched on its own rocket. It is believed to carry a powerful **optical camera**.

36088.fact: The first of **eight** SJ-11 satellites. China never said what they are for; experts guess **missile tracking and early warning**, or listening in on signals.

37166.fact: One of the **first pico-satellites** China launched successfully: a **15 cm cube** weighing 3.5 kg, built by Zhejiang University, with a camera for panoramic views of Earth.

37788.fact: A **10 kg** Italian teaching satellite from Sapienza University of Rome. It also tested a way to **drag itself out of orbit** without any fuel.

38709.fact: A **100 kg** Canadian satellite that listens for the **position signals ships broadcast**, watching traffic through busy shipping lanes and harbours.

38756.fact: Built by students and teachers at the **Osaka Institute of Technology** to show a tiny satellite could steer with an **electric rocket engine**, and to photograph the Osaka area.

39208.fact: Reported to carry a **robotic arm** experiment. It manoeuvred near other satellites and later **released a smaller satellite** of its own.

39358.fact: Officially it probes the **space environment**, measuring radiation and its effects, from an orbit tilted about **75 degrees** to the equator.

39422.fact: A **150 kg** Korean science satellite with an **infrared camera** for imaging our galaxy, plus a small **electric thruster** to test.

39430.fact: A 2 kg CubeSat built to prove that the **position signals from aeroplanes** can be heard from space, so flights over the oceans can be tracked.

39446.fact: A **1 kg** cube from the University of Würzburg that tested a tiny system for **pointing itself**, using magnets and one very small spinning wheel.

39767.fact: A **50 kg** satellite from Wakayama University, a first step towards a fleet of small satellites that could spot **wildfires** quickly.

40015.fact: **Hodoyoshi** is Japanese for **reasonable reliability**: a University of Tokyo idea to make small satellites far cheaper by not over-engineering them.

40025.fact: A 2 kg test run for **QB50**, a plan to launch **50 university CubeSats** to study the little-explored lower thermosphere. It also carries a radio relay for amateurs.

40044.fact: The **very first Lemur**, the standard design of the company Spire. Spire began as a startup called NanoSatisfi, partly paid for by a **Kickstarter** campaign.

40075.fact: A Norwegian **cube just 20 cm wide**, built in Canada. It listens for the radio signals ships send out to say who and where they are.

40136.fact: An experimental satellite for **multimedia communications**, built by **Tsinghua University** with a Beijing telecom company.

41789.fact: A **4 kg** CubeSat that Algerian students learned to build with the University of Surrey. It tested a boom that pops out to **2 metres** from a box the size of a cigarette pack.

43798.fact: A **4 kg** Swiss test for a network that lets small devices anywhere on Earth send short messages, about **1 KB a day**, straight to space.

48908.fact: One of two satellites testing **laser links** between satellites. Its launch slipped after the release mechanism **fired by accident**, damaging both payloads.

40717.fact: One of **three** identical satellites spaced evenly around the same orbit, so together they can photograph **anywhere on Earth once a day**, with details down to 1 metre.

46278.fact: Nicknamed **Iris**. Less than a week after launch it measured **methane** leaking from a gas facility in Turkmenistan, and it can spot leaks far smaller than earlier satellites could.

56186.fact: Nicknamed **Océane**: GHGSat names its methane-hunting satellites after the **children of its team members**. It was built in Toronto.

49772.fact: A **56 kg** BlackSky satellite whose camera sees details about **1 metre** across. It is part of a fleet built for fast, repeated looks at the same places.

52161.fact: A small Norwegian defence test of relaying **UHF radio calls** by satellite at high latitudes, in Norway’s **High North**.

54045.fact: One of **three** satellites launched together. China says they survey land, crops and disasters; outside experts think they are also used for **military reconnaissance**.

55011.fact: Listens for the **radio signals ships give off**, day or night and in any weather, to find and track vessels at sea, even **“dark” ships**.

57422.fact: Built to test flying in **very low orbit**. After launch it used its own **ion thrusters** to lower its orbit, and it carries test cameras.

58295.fact: A **space delivery van**. In February 2024 it released a small satellite into its own orbit, the company’s first **“last-mile” delivery** in space.

59129.fact: The **first satellite** from the young company Apex. It went from a blank-sheet design to working in orbit in about **one year**, which Apex calls a record.

60454.fact: Carries an **infrared camera** that works day and night to spot **fires and volcanoes**, plus a sensor testing ultraviolet levels for India’s Gaganyaan crew capsule.

61784.fact: Built by **Samara University** to measure Earth’s **magnetic field** and the ionosphere. Radio amateurs in 22 countries picked up its holiday greetings.

62394.fact: **Croatia’s first satellite**: a 10 cm cube weighing **1.1 kg**, built over three years by dozens of **volunteers**.

62621.fact: One of **36 SuperDoves** Planet launched at once, on a single SpaceX rideshare that carried **131 spacecraft** in total.

63209.fact: **Tianyan** means **“Sky Eye”** in Chinese. It is listed as an Earth-watching satellite, launched alongside the imaging satellite Siwei Gaojing 3-02.

66376.fact: One of **three** satellites launched together for **“orbital technology testing”**. China has not said what they actually do.

67685.fact: Designed and built entirely at **UPAEP university** in Puebla, Mexico, to keep watch on **active volcanoes**. It is Mexico’s second fully homegrown nanosatellite.

68828.fact: A Russian military **imaging** satellite flying very low, only about **300 km** up. It reached orbit on a light **Angara-1.2** rocket.

46.fact: Secretly a **spy satellite**. Its Sun experiment was a cover story: it also caught **Soviet radar signals**, making it the first satellite ever to spy from orbit.

226.fact: Shaped like an **18-sided drum** about a metre wide and covered in about **9,000 solar cells**. Two TV cameras photographed clouds until one failed in May 1962.

506.fact: A **space dust counter**. Gas-filled cells leaked when a speck of rock punched through them, and one sensor logged **15,000 tiny impacts** by July 1963.

728.fact: Hung a fist-sized ball from an **8.5-metre metal tape**. Gravity pulled the tape straight, and fluid in the ball calmed the wobbles until the satellite **pointed straight down**.

801.fact: Really **Transit 5C-1**, a US Navy navigation satellite. Ships worked out where they were by listening to how its radio tone **changed pitch** as it flew past.

1291.fact: Shared its rocket with **seven other satellites**. With no recorder on board, it beamed its **Sun X-ray readings** live to stations around the world, including one in Italy.

1506.fact: A shiny **aluminium ball** with nine spring-out antennas. US Army surveyors timed radio signals to it to place **islands and continents** on one accurate world map.

1738.fact: Watched the Sun’s **X-rays and ultraviolet light**. On 20 May 1966 it may have become the **first satellite to observe a solar eclipse**.

1982.fact: Powered by about **10,000 solar cells**. Its cameras photographed **Hurricanes Alma, Dorothy and Inez** and Typhoon Judy from space in 1966.

2150.fact: Studied the **radiation belts**, zones of fast particles trapped by Earth’s magnetism. It was one of the few Air Force Orbiting Vehicles to get **a rocket all to itself**.

2610.fact: In 1967 it detected **protons streaming out** of Earth’s upper atmosphere. Scientists interpreted the findings as evidence of an **electric field** helping particles escape into space.

2807.fact: Really **Transit-O 13**, a Navy navigation satellite. It turned out to be one of the toughest of its kind, working for **more than 20 years**.

2920.fact: A secret Air Force **weather satellite**. Its tape recorder stored a daily picture of the **whole northern hemisphere**, and it beamed weather straight to small army and ship receivers.

3174.fact: Built to last a year, but its **battery overcharged and burst** after just a few days. It still sent back about **24 hours of data** about radiation.

4168.fact: A plain sphere with **no power supply at all**. Navy scientists used it to test whether **black paint** could keep a satellite at the right temperature.

5560.fact: Tested a **roll-up solar panel** 4.57 metres long. In the end a command to switch off its radio failed, and it **wore itself out transmitting**.

11081.fact: The rocket stage that carried the CAMEO experiment. It released **clouds of glowing barium gas** high above the polar regions so scientists could watch how they drifted.

13777.fact: Its telescope was chilled with helium to about **-271 °C** to see heat in space. It found **six comets** and Phaethon, the asteroid behind the **Geminid meteor shower**.

20436.fact: Its cameras could see things **10 metres** across. Built to last three years, it kept photographing Earth until **2009**.

21527.fact: Tested how the upper air **bends and garbles radio signals**. It kept one side facing Earth using a **6-metre boom** with a weight on the end.

22825.fact: Carried a **radio relay for hobbyists**, and gave a US weather agency a way to send messages **from the South Pole**. A model of it is in the Smithsonian.

22996.fact: Measured the **harsh radiation** in space and how it upsets computer chips. It rode the **very first Long March 3A** rocket.

23751.fact: Its sharpest camera could spot things about **6 metres** across and tilt sideways to take **3D pictures**. It worked for almost 12 years.

23940.fact: Measured the **ozone layer**, Earth’s natural sunscreen. Rocket failures delayed it two years, so it was flown **lower than planned** to see finer detail.

25693.fact: The **first test** of Surrey Satellite Technology’s bigger ‘minisatellite’ design. It carried cameras, GPS and a **radio relay for hobbyists**.

26385.fact: Ten Chinese engineers spent a year in **England** building it with Surrey Satellite Technology. It tested cameras for a planned **disaster-watching** fleet.

26931.fact: Built by **US Naval Academy** students. It relayed GPS positions from boats and travellers far from anywhere, using a radio hobby system called **APRS**.

932.fact: Shared its rocket with **Explorer 24**, a balloon folded up on top of it. It measured particles **raining into the atmosphere** and is expected to stay in orbit for about **200 years**.

3673.fact: A small box-shaped **listening satellite**, about **95 kg**, flown for the US spy agency NRO. It collected **radar and radio signals** from orbit.

4221.fact: **West Germany’s first** science satellite. It measured the **radiation belts** around Earth and the particles from the Sun that light up the northern lights.

4419.fact: An early Soviet **weather satellite**. Besides a TV camera for clouds it carried an **infrared camera** that sensed heat instead of light, scanning strips 1,000 km wide.

4953.fact: Part of the sixth version of America’s secret **military weather satellites**. Three small Navy test payloads rode up on the **same rocket**.

6019.fact: A **Zaliv** satellite, part of **Tsiklon**, the Soviet Union’s first satellite navigation system. Like an early GPS, it worked by measuring how its radio tone changed pitch.

6236.fact: The first satellite built by **AMSAT**, a club of radio hobbyists. Running on just **3.5 watts** of solar power, it relayed amateurs' signals for nearly five years.

6787.fact: America’s military **weather satellites** were **top secret** until April 1973, a few months before this one launched. That December the programme got its public name, DMSP.

7209.fact: One of the first generation of **Soviet weather satellites**. It weighed about **2,200 kg** and had two solar panels that could swivel to face the Sun.

7476.fact: A **Zaliv** navigation satellite: a drum about **3 metres tall** with a long boom that used **gravity** to keep it pointed at Earth.

7714.fact: Besides photographing clouds, it measured how much **sunlight Earth reflects** and how much heat it gives off, the balance that sets our **climate**.

8197.fact: Shaped like a **gem**: an eight-sided drum with a pyramid on each end, about **90 cm** tall and covered in solar cells. It tested Japan’s satellite tracking and control.

8873.fact: A **Zaliv** satellite from the first Soviet navigation system. Its electronics sat inside a **sealed, pressurized** compartment instead of being open to space.

10095.fact: Rode the **very first Tsyklon-3 rocket**. It was a **Tselina-D** spy satellite, built to listen for radio and radar transmitters on the ground.

10703.fact: Hitched a ride with **Landsat 3**. Built by radio hobbyists, it carried **two radio relays** that amateurs used to talk to each other for more than five years.

11896.fact: Carried **three radio relays** for **civilian** communications. Its antennas sat on **telescopic arms**, and each had its own optical tracker to keep it aimed at Earth.

12818.fact: Really a **Molniya-3** communications satellite, but its launch **only partly succeeded** and it went into the records under a plain Kosmos name.

14670.fact: China’s **first try** at a satellite that hovers over one spot on Earth. A rocket failure left it in the **wrong orbit**, but a twin made it that April.

15429.fact: Relayed **military** phone and telegraph links for the Soviet armed forces. Sturdier radio tubes let it last **three years** instead of two.

16191.fact: Opened the **third generation** of Soviet weather satellites. Later sisters in the series even carried an American **ozone instrument** from NASA.

16881.fact: An **Okean** ocean-watching satellite. Its **side-looking radar** scanned strips of sea 450 km wide, and one satellite could map the whole **Russian Arctic** in 3 to 5 days.

17527.fact: Japan’s **first ocean-watching satellite**. Built to work for two years, it measured sea temperatures and spotted **red tides** for many years longer.

18312.fact: One of 21 **Meteor-2** weather satellites. It carried TV-style cameras for visible and infrared light, plus a sensor for **radiation in space**.

19071.fact: A Navy **Transit** navigation satellite, launched **stacked on top of a twin**. Spares like it were stored in orbit, ready to be switched on when needed.

19807.fact: A Soviet **military** relay satellite. Each of its two antennas had its own **optical tracker** to keep it pointed at Earth during its long, looping orbit.

20478.fact: A follow-up to Japan’s first **ocean-watching satellite**, with the same three sensors. It measured sea temperature, water vapour and **sea ice** until its batteries wore out in 1996.

20682.fact: One of a **trio of Navy spy satellites** flying in a triangle. Comparing when a ship’s radar signal reached each one let them **pinpoint the ship** at sea.

20978.fact: Its rocket left it short of the **orbit it was meant for**, but the Air Force put it to work anyway, watching clouds for military **weather forecasts**.

21799.fact: Part of a **flying triangle** of Navy satellites that tracked ships by their radar. Photographers have caught trios like this gliding past the Moon and the **Pleiades**.

23533.fact: **Blew apart** on 3 February 2015 when a faulty battery burst. It left more than **50,000 tiny pieces** of debris in orbit.

25397.fact: Built by students at Israel’s **Technion** university. The first copy was lost when its rocket failed in 1995, so this one was their **second try**, and it worked.

25560.fact: Searched clouds in space for **water and oxygen**. Switched off in 2004, it was **woken up in 2005** to watch NASA’s Deep Impact probe smash into a comet.

25791.fact: Hunted for **deuterium**, a heavy kind of hydrogen made in the **Big Bang**. Planned to last three and a half years, it worked for more than eight.

25994.fact: Its name, Latin for **Earth**, was chosen in a NASA naming contest for **high school students**. It was the flagship of NASA’s fleet for studying our planet’s climate.

26093.fact: A **200-gram** radio beacon built by Santa Clara University students and launched **from inside another satellite**, OPAL. No signal was ever heard from it.

26609.fact: Its rocket motor **apparently exploded** in December 2000, leaving it in an orbit it wasn’t designed for. Radio amateurs still used it until its **battery failed** in 2004.

27005.fact: Has **no instruments at all**, just **32 glass prisms** on a frame. Ground lasers bounce off them to practise tracking and identifying **space junk**.

27422.fact: Two tiny radio payloads bolted to a used-up **Ariane rocket stage**. One played recorded messages in **four languages**, proving old stages can carry experiments.

27560.fact: Built at a Russian **military academy** to train students, on a satellite frame **left over** from an old communications programme. It also carried a radio for hobbyists.

27608.fact: Built by students and teachers at **Sapienza University of Rome**. Its main job was testing a **tiny thruster** for steering very small satellites.

27840.fact: Not a working satellite: a **dummy** of Russia’s Monitor-E that stayed attached to its rocket stage. It rode up with **eight small satellites**, including Canada’s MOST space telescope.

27941.fact: Nigeria’s part in the **Disaster Monitoring Constellation**, a team of small satellites from seven countries that share pictures to help **aid efforts** around the world.

28545.fact: A **3.6-tonne stand-in** for a real satellite on an Ariane 5 test flight. It carried experiments too, including cameras that filmed key moments of the launch.

28891.fact: A 90 kg British test that took pictures sharp enough to show things **2.5 metres** across and sent them **straight down** to small ground stations below.

28058.fact: A small **store-and-forward** satellite: it picks up messages, carries them around the world and drops them off later. It was finished in 2002 but **waited over a year** to launch.

28413.fact: Launched as a **pair** with a twin to study radiation and conditions in space. Outside experts suspect the pairs also tested **signal-listening** technology.

28982.fact: One of three small NASA test satellites that flew together. During a **‘lights out’** test they ran for a time on **pre-programmed commands**, with no help from the ground.

29107.fact: Its **radar** sliced through clouds to show their height and inside structure, giving the **first global** measurements of this kind. Planned for two years, it lasted 18.

29522.fact: Its cameras could see clouds lit only by a **half moon**, and infrared sensors let it watch weather in **total darkness** for military forecasters.

31118.fact: Bigger than earlier Saudi satellites, it carried sharp **Earth cameras** built with help from a company in **South Africa**.

31129.fact: A **CubeSat** built by Cal Poly students to turn itself using only **magnets** in its side panels. It reached orbit, but no signals were ever heard from it.

32062.fact: The only one of the first three China-Brazil satellites with a **high-resolution camera**. Another, wide camera could cover the whole Earth in about **5 days**.

32790.fact: Only **3.5 kg**, about the size of a **milk carton**. Built at the University of Toronto, it tested tiny thrusters and GPS for satellites that **fly in formation**.

33313.fact: One of five identical satellites flying in a line about **19 minutes apart**, so together they could reach almost any spot on Earth **every day**.

33396.fact: Also called **Thaichote**. It could photograph any part of Thailand within **two days**, helping with maps, farming, forests and **flood risk**.

35931.fact: Tracked **plankton blooms** by the colour of the sea, and measured the **speed and direction of winds** blowing over the oceans.

36797.fact: A **6 kg** cube just 20 cm wide. It listened for ships’ **identity beacons**, which normally reach only about 50 km from shore, to track vessels far out at sea.

37167.fact: One of the **first tiny satellites** China launched successfully: a **15 cm cube** built at Zhejiang University, with a camera for wide views of Earth.

37387.fact: Carried **three cameras**, from sharp close-ups to wide views, plus a receiver that picked up **ships’ location signals** from space.

37789.fact: A **300 kg** imaging satellite whose deal included **training** Nigerian engineers. Its pictures help with maps, farming, water supplies and **disasters**.

37839.fact: A **3 kg** CubeSat built by students at **IIT Kanpur**. Its near-infrared camera was meant to watch **crops and plants** from orbit.

38008.fact: One of **four small spy satellites** flying a few kilometres apart. By combining what each one heard, France could **pinpoint radar stations** around the world.

38761.fact: A **student-built CubeSat** from the University of Colorado. It measured speedy particles from **solar flares** and in Earth’s radiation belts.

39086.fact: Its name stands for **Satellite with ARgos and ALtiKa**. Its radar measured the **height of the sea surface**, the size of waves and the speed of the wind.

39152.fact: A **4 kg** CubeSat from Istanbul Technical University. It worked as a **voice relay** for radio users and carried a small camera too.

39209.fact: A small **store-and-forward** messenger: it collects data from stations on the ground, carries it around the planet and passes it on later.

39423.fact: A **10 kg** cube built for a weather company to watch **Arctic shipping routes**. It also shone **lasers** at Earth to test measuring carbon dioxide.

39678.fact: Its camera could see details **1 metre** across, and it used **ion engines** to reach its final orbit. Sadly it was lost after only **one year**.

39768.fact: A Japanese test of **laser communication**: sending data on beams of light instead of radio waves, with a transmitter small enough for **tiny satellites**.

40016.fact: Carried a NASA experiment using **ultraviolet LEDs** to clear electric charge from a floating test weight, technology for future **gravitational-wave** observatories.

40028.fact: A **3 kg** CubeSat from Singapore. It tested a sharp camera and **tiny gas jets** for turning itself around in space.

40053.fact: In 2014 Airbus **handed it over to Azerbaijan**, which renamed it **Azersky**. Its cameras can pick out things about **2 metres** across.

40718.fact: Used an **off-the-shelf camera** and a small telescope to shoot **video of Earth** from space, showing things as small as **1.5 metres** across.

41337.fact: A powerful **X-ray telescope** that lasted only weeks. A faulty sensor made it think it was turning, and its fixes **spun it so fast that pieces broke off**.

41790.fact: Measured **winds over the oceans** to help forecast weather and **track cyclones**. About 40% of it was built from **spare parts** left over from earlier satellites.

46320.fact: A **6U CubeSat**, about shoebox size, built in the Netherlands for the **Royal Thai Air Force**. It also tested a new camera aiming to see details **5 metres** across.

61769.fact: The **first satellite** built by the Iranian company SpaceOMID. Its camera can see things about **3.5 metres** across and was designed for **farm and land mapping**.

39431.fact: A **10 kg** space telescope that measures how the **brightest stars** change in brightness, about **10 times more precisely** than is possible from the ground.

40076.fact: The **first** joint British satellite launched after the **UK Space Agency** was set up. It carried many test gadgets and later opened a **drag sail** to help it fall from orbit.

36596.fact: Practised **meeting other satellites** in space. In August 2010 it closed in on another Chinese satellite, SJ-6F, and the two may even have **touched**.

38257.fact: Officially a ‘remote sensing’ satellite, but experts think it is an **optical spy satellite**. It flies fairly low, at about **470 km**, to see more detail.

52422.fact: BRO stands for **Breizh Reconnaissance Orbiter**, after the Breton name for Brittany. These **6 kg** satellites pick up radio signals from ships and planes to watch sea traffic.

58296.fact: The **first** of Planet’s **Pelican** satellites, a new generation built to replace SkySat. It photographs Earth in five colours, and Hall-effect thrusters help it move.

61745.fact: A CubeSat from **St Petersburg Polytechnic University**. The series scans **radio noise** coming from Earth’s surface, which can help predict problems with radio, TV and navigation.

42845.fact: Lemur stands for **Low Earth orbit Multi-Use Receiver**. It listens to **GPS signals** bending through the air to work out temperature and humidity for weather forecasts.

58336.fact: A Spire **Lemur** CubeSat. Newer Lemurs like this listen for **aircraft position signals** as well as ships’ radio beacons, tracking traffic all over the globe.

59146.fact: Spire’s Lemurs catch the radio **ID signals** that ships broadcast, so vessels can be followed even **far out at sea**, beyond the reach of coastal stations.

55012.fact: A **3U CubeSat** from Turkish company Plan-S. It tested **Internet of Things** links: short two-way messages between machines, such as remote sensors.

48931.fact: Flies in a **cluster of three** that work together to find where radio signals on Earth come from. The same trick could help locate **emergency beacons** faster.

22626.fact: A **spy satellite** that carried an experimental payload to **eavesdrop on communication links**, not just radar. It was the fourth and last of its type.

24728.fact: **Gonets** means ‘messenger’. It stored messages and passed them on later, and the system was even offered to help send **medical records** to remote places.

39251.fact: Catches messages as it passes over one place and delivers them over another. Gonets satellites like this one were launched **three at a time** on a single rocket.

40063.fact: A civilian version of Russia’s military **Strela-3M** satellites. People could send it messages from a **handheld terminal** that looked like a mobile phone.

40553.fact: Flies about **1,500 km** up, more than three times higher than the space station, so each pass covers a huge area as it **collects and delivers messages**.

39497.fact: A secret satellite that **wasn’t announced** at launch, which muddled the Kosmos numbering. It carried a **radio for hobbyists** and broke apart in January 2020.

40922.fact: A military **store-and-forward** satellite: it records messages as it passes one station and delivers them over another. It was one of **three launched on one rocket**.

41032.fact: The **first** of Russia’s new **Tundra** satellites, which watch for **missile launches**. They are reported to carry an emergency radio link for use in a nuclear war.

54109.fact: A **classified** Russian military satellite whose job has never been revealed. It was launched together with a companion, Kosmos 2562.

40137.fact: The fourth of China’s small **Chuangxin 1** messenger satellites, which pick up data from remote stations and relay it later. Chuangxin means **‘innovation’**.

36110.fact: Thought to be a camera-carrying **spy satellite** that works alongside **radar** satellites of the same family, which can see through clouds.

39012.fact: Flies in a **trio**, much like America’s Navy ocean-watching satellites. Experts believe these Chinese trios track **ships at sea**.

40338.fact: One of **three satellites launched together** that fly in formation about **1,090 km** up. Experts think they are China’s version of America’s ship-hunting NOSS trios.

39410.fact: Belongs to a newer class of Chinese **optical spy satellites** that fly unusually high, about **1,200 km** up. Its camera came from an optics institute in Changchun.

22076.fact: Measured the **height of the sea surface** across the world’s oceans every **ten days**, with record accuracy, showing how ocean currents flow. A joint NASA and French mission.

41599.fact: The first Cartosat-2 to add a **colour camera**. It also flew lower, at about **505 km**, to see finer detail on the ground.

41773.fact: Packs a telescope with a **3.6-metre focal length** into a small satellite, sharp enough to spot things about **1 metre** across.

49949.fact: Its camera can make out things about **1 metre** across, and satellites like it can take up to **1,000 pictures a day**.

56202.fact: Named after **Maria Gaetana Agnesi**, an Italian mathematician of the 1700s. It is a **37.5 kg** camera satellite that can see things about 1 metre across.

41877.fact: A near-copy of Resourcesat-2, built so there would be **no gap** in India’s land pictures. Its sharpest camera covers strips **70 km** wide.

28369.fact: One of Saudi Arabia’s first small **store-and-forward** communication satellites, weighing just **12 kg**. Seven other satellites shared its rocket.

39448.fact: Not a separate satellite: a box of **test navigation gear** bolted to the rocket’s top stage and powered by the **rocket’s own batteries**. Dozens of satellites shared that launch.

23342.fact: Its scanners pictured land in visible light and **heat**, and it carried a small German **data-messaging** experiment called Safir. It worked for six years.

33751.fact: Part of **Europe’s first test** of spotting **missile launches** from space by the heat of their rockets. It flew a stretched orbit reaching out to about **36,000 km**.

33494.fact: Built by Tohoku University to study **sprites**, flashes of light high above thunderstorms. Renamed **Raijin** after reaching orbit, it failed after just 12 days.

41896.fact: Gave the **first proof** that ‘chorus’ radio waves in space knock electrons down into the air, the cause of flickering **pulsating auroras**.

38711.fact: The **first** satellite built on Lavochkin’s small **Karat** design. Its radio sensor measured **ocean saltiness** and soil moisture, and mapped polar sea ice.

13011.fact: A test capsule that rode the **fourth flight** of Europe’s Ariane 1 rocket, sharing the trip with **MARECS A**, a satellite for ship communications.

35684.fact: A **12 kg** satellite run for exactEarth, a Canadian ship-tracking company. It picked up ships’ **position signals** from space and relayed data for tracking equipment.

24926.fact: A **pretend Iridium satellite**: a mass model flown on the first Long March 2C/SD, to prove the rocket could carry satellites for the **Iridium** phone network.

60511.fact: One of a batch of **36 Planet Doves** launched together on one rideshare rocket. Each is a small 3U CubeSat weighing about **5.7 kg**.
