61785.fact: Built by a Moscow technology university with the company Geoscan. It tests a **GLONASS/GPS receiver** for studying the upper air and a radio link to **talk to another CubeSat**.

67686.fact: A **1.1 kg** CubeSat from Malaysia’s UiTM university, released from the space station’s **Kibo** module. It tests collecting sensor data from **remote areas** with no phone network.

57429.fact: Catalogued as **AS-03**, a commercial Earth-imaging satellite for the Chinese company Skysight. It launched with two sisters and a flat-panel communications test satellite.

63212.fact: The **first satellite** of Spanish company Startical. This 16U CubeSat tests whether air traffic controllers can **talk to planes through space** using aircraft radio.

62628.fact: A D-Orbit **space tug**: it carries a load of small satellites and releases each one into its own orbit. Each ION also gets a person’s name, like **‘Joyful Julia’**.

69328.fact: From **Shenzhou-22**, a spaceship sent up with **no crew** as a lifeboat after another Shenzhou’s window cracked, possibly hit by space debris. It also carried repair gear.

68829.fact: A secret Russian military satellite launched on a small **Angara-1.2** rocket. It flies very low, only about **330 km** up, on a path that passes near both poles.

58.fact: The world’s first **active repeater** communications satellite: it stored messages and sent them on. Its first job was relaying a message from **President Eisenhower** to the United Nations.

309.fact: Shaped like an **18-sided drum** covered in about **9,000 solar cells**. Little rockets kept it spinning like a top while its TV camera photographed clouds for forecasters.

573.fact: Besides relaying TV signals across the ocean, it measured radiation in the **Van Allen belts**. In France it was tracked by a huge antenna under a **50-metre dome** that is now a museum.

729.fact: SECOR stands for **Sequential Collation of Range**. Radio signals flashed between it and portable ground stations to fix exact positions, tying **islands and continents** onto one map.

812.fact: From the first family of US **military weather satellites**. This spinning 10-sided box photographed clouds over Europe and Asia for the Air Force weather centre at **Strategic Air Command**.

959.fact: Its ultraviolet telescope made the **first full survey of the stars in ultraviolet light** from orbit, in 1965. It also mapped Earth’s magnetic field with a sensor on a long pole.

1292.fact: Officially a gravity experiment, it was also **Poppy 4D**, a secret US satellite built to pick up the signals of **Soviet radars** and send them home for analysis.

1510.fact: Nicknamed **Porcupine**: a small ball that pushed out **12 rods**, each over 7 metres long, giving radar stations a big target to practise tracking.

1778.fact: France’s very first satellite. It made France only the **third country** to put a satellite up on **its own rocket**, and it is expected to stay in orbit for **centuries**.

2016.fact: Named after the French word for a **tuning fork**. Scientists tracked its radio signal and photographed it against the stars for over **five years** to measure the Earth precisely.

2173.fact: Shaped like a giant **ocean buoy**, nearly 4 metres tall. It tested new cameras and **infrared sensors** that measure heat rising from Earth and its clouds, for better weather forecasts.

2657.fact: It beamed cloud photos **instantly** to weather stations below using **Automatic Picture Transmission** cameras. One camera failed after launch, but the other worked fine.

2826.fact: Calsphere 3: a **4.5 kg metal ball** with no power or radio at all. Radars bounce signals off it to check they measure correctly. It shared its rocket with **four Poppy spy satellites**.

2965.fact: A **Transit** navigation satellite for the US Navy. From this batch on, Transits lasted **more than 14 years** on average, far longer than the 14 months expected.

3229.fact: Part of **Tsiklon**, the Soviet Union’s **first satellite navigation system**. Users worked out where they were from the way its radio signal changed pitch as it passed over.

3764.fact: Covered in **10,020 solar cells**, it rolled around its orbit like a **cartwheel**, photographing each part of Earth’s clouds once a day. It worked for almost **five years**.

4237.fact: This was **Poppy 6B**, one of four secret US Navy satellites launched together to record the radio signals of **Soviet radars**.

4320.fact: The test model for a new, improved kind of weather satellite. Besides four TV cameras, it had **infrared** scanners that sense the heat of clouds, which works even **in the dark**.

4507.fact: A **Transit** navigation satellite built by RCA. Transits lasted so long that unused spares were packed into a row of grey boxes nicknamed **the long grey line**.

5104.fact: Its radio antenna stretched **73 metres**, longer than a hockey rink, to probe the layer of charged air high above us. When Canada switched it off in 1984, **Japan** turned it back on.

5580.fact: The first satellite launched on a **British rocket**, Black Arrow. The rocket’s last stage kept firing after letting go, bumped into it and **knocked off an antenna**.

6079.fact: From the **first family** of Soviet weather satellites. Its TV camera photographed a strip of clouds about **1,000 km wide** as it passed overhead.

6256.fact: Besides a TV camera, this Meteor carried an **infrared camera** that sees the warmth of clouds, so it could keep watching the weather on Earth’s **night side**.

6828.fact: A **Zaliv** navigation satellite: an 800 kg drum about 2 metres wide, kept pointing at Earth by a long **gravity boom** sticking out of it.

7213.fact: Named after a character in Shakespeare’s **The Tempest**, like Prospero before it. It tested steering itself with little puffs of **propane gas**.

7490.fact: Besides watching the weather, it tested an **SPD-60 plasma thruster**, a gentle engine that pushes with a stream of electrically charged gas.

7734.fact: Its **radar altimeter** measured its height above the ocean to within tens of centimetres, helping scientists map the true **shape of the sea surface** and Earth’s gravity.

8293.fact: Besides cloud cameras, it measured **sunlight bouncing off Earth** and the heat Earth gives off, clues to how our planet’s energy stays in balance.

9057.fact: The **last** of the improved TIROS weather satellites. It unfolded **three curved solar panels**, each over 4 metres long, and measured the air’s temperature at different heights.

10457.fact: A Transit satellite rebuilt to pretend to be a **Trident missile** in flight. It passed on **GPS signals** so the Navy could test the system that made its missiles more accurate.

10731.fact: One of the **last** satellites of Tsiklon, the first Soviet navigation system. Later the job passed to the military **Parus** and civilian **Tsikada** satellites.

11084.fact: A **dummy** weather satellite used to test the new Tsiklon-3 rocket. Riding along were **RS-1 and RS-2**, the first Soviet satellites for amateur radio fans.

11962.fact: From the **second generation** of Soviet weather satellites, weighing about **1,300 kg**. It scanned clouds in visible and infrared light from about 900 km up.

12848.fact: Its name means a **halo of light**, after the auroras it studied. It carried **12 experiments**, seven from France, to learn how space energy pours into the sky near the poles.

13012.fact: Molniya is Russian for **lightning**, after how fast it whips past Earth at the low point of its stretched orbit. It then lingers high over the far north, where Russia needed coverage.

13875.fact: A **Molniya-3**, the version made for civilian communications. Its orbit swung out to about **40,000 km** over the north and back in to 500 km every 12 hours.

14780.fact: Guinness calls it the **longest-working Earth-watching satellite** ever: built to last 3 years, it worked for **29**. It was the first satellite to capture the **Chernobyl** disaster.

15516.fact: A Meteor-2 launched on the newer **Tsiklon-3** rocket. Besides cloud pictures, it measured the **radiation** in space around Earth.

16393.fact: Its six solar panels always faced the **Sun**, while two antennas on **telescopic arms** swivelled to keep pointing at Earth.

16909.fact: Built by the **Japan Amateur Radio League**, this 26-sided satellite rode the **first flight** of Japan’s H-I rocket. Radio hobbyists used it to swap messages worldwide.

17589.fact: Not a working satellite but a **3,250 kg stand-in**: a copy of a Soviet spy satellite loaded with extra weight to prove the new **Zenit-2** rocket could lift heavy loads.

18361.fact: A Transit navigation satellite launched **stacked on top of another** on one small rocket, then kept in orbit as a spare. After 1996 it was used to study the **ionosphere**.

19223.fact: An upgraded Transit navigation satellite with tiny **plasma thrusters** that fired to cancel the drag of thin air, keeping its orbit steady for years.

19851.fact: Unlike the US, which kept separate civilian and military weather satellites, the Soviet Union used **one type for both**. Meteor-2 satellites like this did both jobs.

20437.fact: Built at the **University of Surrey**, it worked as a **digital post office** in orbit, storing messages and passing them on. That’s handy for remote or disaster-hit places.

20479.fact: Orizuru means **folded paper crane**. It tested opening and closing an **umbrella** in space, an idea for using thin air as a brake.

20691.fact: One of a **trio** of secret US satellites flying together. By comparing when each one heard a radio signal, they could **pinpoint ships and aircraft** far out at sea.

21087.fact: Besides gathering data from science stations, it carried **RS-14**, an amateur radio built jointly by Soviet and **German** radio hobbyists.

21574.fact: Its radar measured the sea surface so precisely that scientists used it to map the shape of the **ocean floor** hidden below. It worked for **nine years** until a gyroscope failed.

21808.fact: From the second generation of US ocean-watching spy satellites, much heavier than the first. Besides tracking ships by their radios, they could **recognise certain foreign communications**.

22077.fact: South Korea’s **first satellite**, nicknamed “Our Star” (Uribyol). Built with help from Britain’s University of Surrey, it was meant to last five years but kept in touch for **12**.

22671.fact: A **Molniya-1T** carrying radios for the military **Korund** network. More reliable radio tubes meant it was designed to last **three years** instead of two.

22826.fact: Built by Italian radio hobbyists and weighing just **11 kg**. It worked like a **mailbox in orbit**, holding messages from radio amateurs and passing them on.

23105.fact: Launched from under the wing of a **B-52 bomber** on a Pegasus rocket. It ended up in the wrong orbit, but its one experiment still tested new ways to **detect radio signals**.

23411.fact: A Russian **surveying satellite** of about 1,500 kg, with eight panels that open out like **flower petals** for extra power. It helped fix exact positions for maps.

23547.fact: It made the world’s **first wide-area map of lightning**, including flashes between clouds. It also proved that **GPS signals** passing through the air can measure the weather.

23752.fact: A US and **Russian** team-up: American instruments on a body with Russian power and engines. It studied the **ultraviolet glow** made when objects rush through the upper air.

24277.fact: Midori means **green** in Japanese. It watched ozone and greenhouse gases for only **10 months**, until damage to its solar panel sent it out of control.

24729.fact: Gonets means **messenger**. It was offered to health groups to carry **medical records** to remote places, holding messages until it flew over the right ground station.

24954.fact: A test for a planned 26-satellite messaging network. It was **left behind** on an earlier launch because of a paperwork glitch, then rode the next rocket months later.

25175.fact: Kakehashi means **bridge**. Its rocket’s second stage **shut off too early**, stranding it in the wrong orbit, so engineers fired its engine seven times to reach a usable one.

25398.fact: A ball covered in **laser mirrors**, set so only about one reflects at a time. That gives laser stations a sharp target for measuring Earth to the **millimetre**.

25567.fact: Nadezhda means **hope** in Russian. Besides helping ships find their position, it carried **COSPAS** gear that picks up distress beacons from people in trouble.

25730.fact: In 2007 China smashed this weather satellite with a missile in a weapons test. It created the **largest cloud of space junk** in history.

25860.fact: Built in **Ukraine** on the body design of a Soviet spy satellite, this **6,360 kg** giant watched the oceans, sea ice, plants and soil.

26032.fact: Named after **Arirang**, a much-loved Korean folk song. It was the first satellite built mainly by **South Korean engineers**, and its camera could spot things 6.6 metres across.

26086.fact: Not a real satellite: a **dummy** as heavy as two of Europe’s **Cluster** science satellites, attached to a new Fregat rocket stage to prove it could carry them.

26386.fact: A **6.5 kg** nanosatellite with a **butane** thruster the size of a pencil. Right after launch it photographed the satellites it rode up with, then steered toward one of them.

26610.fact: A cube-shaped test satellite for British defence scientists. It tried out new gear like **lithium-ion batteries** and GPS while flying through the harsh **Van Allen radiation belts**.

26932.fact: Built by **Stanford students**, it carried a **voice synthesizer** to speak over the radio, plus a digital camera and new infrared sensors.

27058.fact: A civilian cousin of Russia’s military **Strela-3** satellites, launched on the same rocket as them. It picked up messages from the ground and **delivered them later** elsewhere.

27424.fact: Aqua is Latin for **water**. Its Japanese microwave sensor, AMSR-E, was built to last three years and kept working for **over nine**, until 2011.

27561.fact: An experiment bolted to its rocket’s upper stage. It sent news about the launch to engineers **by e-mail**, relayed through the Orbcomm satellite network.

27609.fact: A **stand-in** for a private Moon probe. The real probe missed this ride because of missing **export paperwork**, so a mock-up of the same size and weight flew instead.

27842.fact: Built by students at the Technical University of Denmark. It carried a **tether** meant to drag it out of orbit, unrolled by a clever **yo-yo** system.

27942.fact: Part of an international team of satellites that photograph **disaster zones**. It carried a **Cisco internet router** and made the first test of the **Interplanetary Internet** in space.

28060.fact: A **980 kg** test of whether ordinary, off-the-shelf parts, the kind used in everyday electronics on Earth, can cope with the harsh conditions of space.

28370.fact: A **12 kg** Saudi satellite that worked like an orbiting **post box**, collecting messages and dropping them off later. It was based on an earlier Saudisat design.

28414.fact: Shi Jian 6 satellites fly in **pairs**. They were said to study radiation in space, though experts suspect they also tested ways to **listen in on radio signals**.

28649.fact: Its two cameras photograph the ground from **two angles** at almost the same moment, like a pair of eyes, so the pictures can be turned into **3D maps**.

28893.fact: **Iran’s first satellite**, built for Iran by a Russian company in Omsk for about **US$15 million** after plans to launch it on an Iranian rocket ran into trouble.

29047.fact: One of **six** Taiwan-US satellites launched on a single rocket. They measured the air by tracking **GPS signals** passing through it, for weather and space-weather research.

29108.fact: It fired a **laser** down through the air to measure clouds and floating dust layer by layer, day and night. The French-American mission lasted **over 17 years**.

29678.fact: The first spacecraft built to hunt **planets around other stars** by watching them dim. It found **CoRoT-7b**, the first such planet shown to be made of rock or metal.

31119.fact: Besides storing and forwarding messages, it carried a receiver for the **position signals ships send out**, so it could help track vessels at sea.

31130.fact: CAPE stands for **Cajun** Advanced Picosatellite Experiment: a 10 cm cube built by Louisiana students, beeping out the radio call sign **K5USL**.

32289.fact: A Chinese **radar** satellite from China’s first family of space radars. Radar sends out its own signals, so it can take pictures through **clouds and darkness**.

32791.fact: A replacement for the first SEEDS, which was **lost when its rocket failed** in 2006. This little cube could **play voice messages** to radio amateurs.

33314.fact: One of **five** satellites launched on one rocket and spaced about **19 minutes** apart in the same orbit, so together they could photograph places often.

33408.fact: One half of the third **Shi Jian 6 pair**: the ‘A’ satellites use a different body design from their ‘B’ partners. Their stated job was measuring **radiation** in space.

33495.fact: Its name means **shining**. It carried messages from **children with disabilities**, who were invited to the launch. Sadly, no signal was ever heard from it.

33752.fact: One of two French test satellites that looked for the **heat of missile launches** against Earth below, Europe’s first trial of a space **early-warning** system.

35685.fact: A **22 kg**, 14-sided Spanish satellite that relayed messages between Spain, research bases in **Antarctica** and the navy ship Hespérides.

35932.fact: **Switzerland’s first satellite**, a 10 cm cube built by students in Lausanne. It photographed **airglow**, the faint light the upper air gives off at night.

36121.fact: The **first** of a new generation of Chinese optical spy satellites, flying unusually high at about **1,200 km**.

36598.fact: Named after **Jean Picard**, a 1600s French astronomer who measured the Sun’s size accurately. This satellite measured the **Sun’s size and brightness** to see how they affect our climate.

36798.fact: A **117 kg** Algerian satellite whose telescope could spot things **2.5 metres** across, helping with maps, farming, water and the search for minerals.

37168.fact: A **watchtower in space**: its camera tracks other satellites and **space junk** from orbit. That data can help keep astronauts’ spacecraft out of harm’s way.

37388.fact: An India-Russia satellite with instruments built partly by **students**. It studied how changes on the **Sun** affect the upper layers of Earth’s air.

37790.fact: A training satellite: Nigerian engineers spent **18 months** in Britain helping design, build and test it, then took charge of it in orbit themselves.

37840.fact: A **29 kg** satellite that picked up the **position signals ships broadcast**, so they could be tracked far out at sea. Built to last 3 years, it kept going about **4**.

38009.fact: One of **four** French test satellites flying a few kilometres apart. By comparing the radar signals each one hears, they can work out **where the radars are**.

38337.fact: Shizuku means **water drop** in Japanese. Its microwave sensor measures rain, water vapour, snow depth, sea temperature and wind over the oceans.

38734.fact: An upgraded **Gonets** messenger satellite. People on the ground can send it data using a handheld terminal that looks a bit like a **mobile phone**.

38764.fact: A small CubeSat built by students in **California, London and Korea**. It was designed to film tiny particles that reveal the **invisible ring** of charged gas circling Earth.

39013.fact: Launched as a **trio** that flies together. Experts think the three team up to **track ships at sea**, much like America’s NOSS ocean-watching satellites.

39088.fact: **Canada’s first dedicated military space mission**: a space telescope that tracks satellites and junk between **6,000 and 40,000 km** up, for the catalogue NORAD uses.

39153.fact: An Argentine CubeSat whose design was shared **freely** so students and radio hobbyists could copy it. It tested a tiny spinning wheel and a camera for future Earth-watching satellites.

39210.fact: A Chinese test satellite reported to be **watching space junk**. It was launched together with two other experimental satellites.

39253.fact: Named after a cape where fishermen prayed for safe trips, its name can also mean **“beyond the Sun”**. It studied planets like **Jupiter** in ultraviolet light from Earth orbit.

39416.fact: Also called **exactView 5R**, it listened for the **position signals ships broadcast**, helping track vessels around the world.

39424.fact: A twin built by South Korea’s **Kyung Hee University** to join the CINEMA team studying the charged particles around Earth. It reached orbit, but **no signals** were ever received.

39432.fact: Built at Pakistan’s Institute of Space Technology, this 1 kg cube was released in orbit by **another satellite**, Italy’s UniSat-5. Sadly **no signals** were ever received.

39451.fact: One of three satellites mapping **Earth’s magnetic field**. When a backup sensor on its sister Charlie had trouble, Bravo was sent to fly **alone in a higher orbit**.

39490.fact: A metal **radar calibration ball**: ground radars aim at it to check they are measuring correctly. It rode the **first-ever flight** of Russia’s Soyuz-2-1v rocket with a twin sphere.

39731.fact: A **900 kg** Earth-imaging satellite run from Kazakhstan by Kazakh operators trained by its European builder. It flew to space on Europe’s small **Vega** rocket.

39769.fact: A second try after **Raijin**, a university satellite that failed after 12 days. Tohoku University built it to watch **sprites**, strange flashes of light high above thunderstorms.

40017.fact: Said to be Russia’s **first privately built satellite**. Its camera could see details **15 metres** across, testing ideas for a future fleet.

40032.fact: A test run for **QB50**, a plan to launch 50 university CubeSats together. It also carried a **voice radio** relay for hobbyists, known as **EO-80**.

40054.fact: A **14 kg** German satellite with a **4-metre** coiled antenna for catching ships’ position signals, even the signals from **rescue beacons**.

40069.fact: A Russian weather satellite hit by a tiny **space rock** in 2019, which damaged its power system. Problems grew until it could no longer point its cameras at Earth.

40109.fact: Part of a trio launched together, probably to **replace** the first Yaogan 9 trio. These teams are thought to keep watch on **ships across the oceans**.

40143.fact: Reportedly the **last** of its family of Chinese optical spy satellites, which flew low, **under 500 km** up.

40339.fact: One of three satellites flying as a group about **1,090 km** up. Like the other Yaogan trios, it is thought to help China’s military **watch ships** at sea.

40554.fact: Launched **three at a time** with fellow Gonets-M satellites on a Rokot rocket. The fleet collects messages and data, then **drops them off** later at stations far away.

40719.fact: It carried a folded **4 by 4 metre sail** meant to catch thin air and drag it out of orbit. Sadly the sail **never opened**, probably because of disconnected motor cables.

40930.fact: **India’s first** dedicated space observatory. Its five instruments see the sky in visible, **ultraviolet and X-ray** light at the same time.

41038.fact: Thought to be the **first** of a new family of Chinese **radar** satellites, with a different shape from the radar satellites it followed.

41338.fact: Built by Nagoya and Daido universities, it carried a **radiation detector**, an **infrared camera** to spot space junk, and a radio relay for amateurs.

41601.fact: Its telescope can make out things about **1 metre** across from roughly 450 km up. The company that designed it, Skybox, was later renamed **Terra Bella** by Google.

41774.fact: One of **four** SkySats launched together on a European **Vega** rocket. Its thrusters use a **“green”** fuel meant to be safer than the usual satellite fuel.

41847.fact: Two small experiments **bolted to a rocket’s last stage** instead of flying free: a test for Chinese **amateur radio** satellites and a gadget tester. They lasted only weeks.

41884.fact: One of **eight** small satellites that measure **winds inside hurricanes** by catching GPS signals that bounce off the stormy sea.

41898.fact: China’s **first** satellite dedicated to measuring **carbon dioxide**, a key gas warming our planet. It reads the gas in sunlight reflected off Earth.

42987.fact: One of six SkySats launched on a **Minotaur-C** rocket. Its camera chip has stripes with **blue, green, red and near-infrared** filters to build colour pictures.

44389.fact: A radar satellite from Finland’s **ICEYE**, the company that first shrank radar imaging satellites to **under 100 kg**. Radar lets it see the ground through **clouds and darkness**.

46457.fact: Launched from a **ship at sea** in a batch of nine Jilin-1 satellites. Some in the batch take sharp photos while others shoot **colour video** of Earth.

48948.fact: One of a **trio** of satellites flying together to pinpoint where radio signals come from on Earth. That can help spot radio **interference** and find **emergency beacons**.

49950.fact: Its small **24 cm telescope** can spot things about **1 metre** across, and satellites like it can take up to **1,000 pictures a day**, as photos or video.

52908.fact: Launched as a trio of **different designs**. Even satellite experts don’t know their job: guesses range from cameras to radar to **listening for signals**.

54251.fact: One of five Jilin-1 satellites launched together on a small **Ceres-1** rocket. Two other satellites of the same type were later **sold to Russia’s Wagner Group**.

55041.fact: From Skykraft’s first launch: an Australian test of satellites that let **air traffic controllers talk to pilots** in real time, wherever the plane is flying.

56203.fact: Its maker, Satellogic, has a tradition of naming satellites after **remarkable women in science**. It is one of a fleet that photographs Earth in **fine detail**.

58018.fact: One of three Spanish CubeSats meant to fly as a team checking the **water quality** of reservoirs in Spain and Portugal. Sadly, the team’s **leader satellite failed to deploy**.

58302.fact: Part of what is now the world’s **largest fleet of radar imaging satellites**, run by a company that began as a spin-off from Finland’s **Aalto University**.

58435.fact: A secret Russian military satellite. Some experts thought it was the first of a new spy type called **Razdan**, but satellite watchers now **aren’t sure** what it really is.

59148.fact: A small satellite with a **hyperspectral camera**, which sees many more shades of colour than our eyes, to watch **Atlantic coasts** and seas as part of a shared satellite network.

60520.fact: An Italian **in-orbit servicing** test: it was designed to manoeuvre around a virtual target. Later missions in the IPERDRONE programme aim to **return cargo safely to Earth**.

61749.fact: A small CubeSat testing **VERA**, a new **plasma thruster**, plus a receiver that uses GPS and GLONASS signals to study the **ionosphere**, the electrically charged upper air.

61771.fact: One of a big batch of Russian **SITRO-AIS** CubeSats that pick up the **position messages ships broadcast** and pass them to the ground, to help keep shipping safe.

61786.fact: Built by the Russian company SPUTNIX for Sitronics. Like its many siblings, it tracks ships by catching the automatic **ID signals** they send out to help **avoid collisions**.

62636.fact: A Planet **Dove**, a camera satellite about the size of a **loaf of bread**. Some Dove pictures are shared as **open data** for climate, farming and disaster work.

67481.fact: Left in orbit by the **Shenzhou 20** crew mission. That spaceship was damaged, probably by **space junk**, so its three astronauts flew home in a different spacecraft.

66906.fact: It tests two tiny thrusters that use **plastic** fed from a spool, like thread, as fuel. The fuel isn’t toxic or under pressure, which makes it **safe to handle**.

67687.fact: Built by students from **17 countries** at Japan’s Kyutech and Singapore’s NTU. It opens its solar panels with **shape-memory metal** instead of springs.

69473.fact: One of two Chinese test satellites for **direct-to-cell** service, beaming signals straight to phones. It rode a Zhuque-2E rocket that burns **methane** and liquid oxygen.

100083.fact: Rassvet means **dawn**. It is one of Russia’s first working satellites for space **internet**, which pass data to each other by **laser** and steer with krypton-gas thrusters.

107.fact: Carried the **first gamma-ray telescope** ever flown in space. It caught just **22 gamma rays** from the sky, the very start of gamma-ray astronomy.

340.fact: Built and paid for by the phone company **AT&T**, not NASA. It beamed the first **live TV between America and Europe**, then radiation from a nuclear test in space knocked it out.

670.fact: Powered by a small **nuclear battery**. It settled into orbit **upside down**, so its signals were too weak for Navy ships to use, but scientists still got useful data from it.

730.fact: Watched the **Sun’s X-rays**, and its readings **dramatically changed** what scientists thought about the corona, the Sun’s glowing outer atmosphere.

813.fact: A secret Air Force **weather satellite**, launched as a pair with its twin. Shaped like a **10-sided drum**, it spun to snap TV pictures of clouds over huge squares of land.

965.fact: One of the Navy’s **Oscar** navigation satellites (O for operational). This one, Oscar 2, was built in Indianapolis and, like Oscar 1, **stopped working within days**.

1293.fact: Earlier OSCARs could only beep “HI” in Morse code. This was the **first that relayed signals** from the ground, passing on messages between radio hams in North America and Europe.

1514.fact: Secretly a Navy **Oscar** navigation satellite (O for operational). The early Indianapolis-built Oscars were not made to spec, and the ones that reached orbit **worked only a few weeks**.

1804.fact: Built from the **spare copy of Alouette 1**, it studied the charged upper air for nearly 10 years. Alouette is French for **skylark**, and the name of a folk song.

2091.fact: Sent cloud photos down **live** as it flew over, using a system called Automatic Picture Transmission. Forecasters got useful pictures from it for **more than four years**.

2176.fact: Navy navigation satellite **Oscar 9**, rebuilt by the Johns Hopkins lab from parts made in Indianapolis. It lasted months instead of weeks, but **workmanship faults** still cut its life short.

2669.fact: A secret military **weather satellite**. Unlike earlier models it had **two tilted TV cameras**, so its cloud pictures finally joined up at the equator with no gaps.

2828.fact: Its public name hid a secret: it was really **Poppy 5B**, a Navy spy satellite that listened for the radar of **Soviet missile defences**.

2980.fact: A secret military weather satellite. Its tape recorder stored pictures of the **whole northern hemisphere** every day, and it could beam weather straight to **small receivers on ships**.

3266.fact: A secret military weather satellite. One more of this exact model was built but never launched, and was donated to Chicago’s **Museum of Science and Industry**.

3825.fact: One of four small research satellites launched together on a single Atlas rocket. Its job was to measure Earth’s **radiation belts**, rings of trapped particles in space.

4247.fact: Secretly **Poppy 6C**, one of four spy satellites flying as a team. By timing when a radar signal reached each one, the team could **pin down where it came from**.

4321.fact: Built by **students at the University of Melbourne**, it was the first amateur satellite that could be **controlled by commands** sent up from the ground.

4512.fact: Its weather programme stayed secret until **April 1973**, when the Air Force revealed it, partly because its cloud pictures were being used in the **Vietnam War**.

5238.fact: Secretly a **Zaliv** satellite for Tsiklon, the Soviet Union’s first navigation system. It was the first Zaliv sent higher, to about **1,000 km** above Earth.

5683.fact: A **Zaliv** navigation satellite, a drum about 3 m tall. Ships worked out where they were from the **changing pitch** of its radio signal as it passed overhead.

6126.fact: Built from a modified **weather satellite**, it was the first to carry a **Multispectral Scanner**, a camera that sees colours of light beyond what our eyes can.

6275.fact: A secret Air Force weather satellite. When the programme came out of hiding, it was renamed the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program, or **DMSP**, in December 1973.

6909.fact: One of the Navy’s **Oscar** navigation satellites, built by RCA. Ships and submarines worked out their position from the **changing pitch** of its radio signal.

7218.fact: The last of five Block 5B military **weather satellites**, and the first of them launched after the once-secret programme went public as **DMSP**.

7529.fact: Instead of TV cameras, it saw clouds with **radiometers** that measure light and heat, so it could map cloud cover **by night** as well as by day.

7768.fact: Secretly a **Zaliv** navigation satellite. Its drum-shaped body was **sealed and filled with air**, so the electronics inside worked in a pressurised room.

8519.fact: Watched clouds with a TV camera by day and an **infrared camera** that saw their heat at night, each covering a strip of Earth about **1,000 km wide**.

9061.fact: Secretly a **Zaliv** navigation satellite. A long boom stuck out from it, letting **gravity keep one side facing Earth** without using any fuel.

10459.fact: One of the last **Zaliv** satellites of Tsiklon, the first Soviet navigation system. Tsiklon was later replaced by the military **Parus** and civilian **Tsikada** satellites.

10820.fact: A military weather satellite that fired its own rocket motors to finish the climb to orbit, so the satellite **acted as its own top rocket stage**.

11085.fact: One of the **first two Soviet amateur radio satellites**, built by a Moscow engineering institute. Battery trouble shut down its radio relay after only a few months.

12295.fact: Rode the **first flight** of Japan’s N-II rocket, which sent it into a long, stretched orbit heading out toward the height where **weather and TV satellites** park.

12997.fact: Built by the radio club of DOSAAF, a Soviet youth training group. It went up with **five sister satellites** on one rocket, as an experiment with no relay open to the public.

13070.fact: Carried radios for the Soviet military network **Korund**. Better tubes in its transmitters doubled the planned life of these satellites from one year to **two years**.

13890.fact: Molniya means **lightning**, a nod to how fast it whips through the low point of its long, looping orbit before slowing down high above the north.

14781.fact: Carried a **speech synthesiser** that could talk over the radio, and a microphone to hear specks of space dust hitting it. Fans still heard its signal **over 40 years** after launch.

15595.fact: Its radar measured the height of the sea surface to within about **5 cm**. Tiny bumps in the ocean revealed the pull of hidden **undersea mountains**.

16408.fact: A second-generation Soviet weather satellite of about **1,300 kg**. It carried three TV-style scanners to watch clouds and a sensor to measure **radiation in nearby space**.

16969.fact: Carried an instrument that measured how much of the Sun’s energy Earth **bounces back and gives off**, plus a receiver for **search-and-rescue** distress beacons.

17997.fact: Not a spy satellite itself but the **mothership**: it carried three Navy ocean-watching satellites to orbit, then released them to fly together in a **triangle**.

18362.fact: Not a ham radio satellite: this Oscar is a Navy **Transit** navigation satellite, launched **stacked on a twin** on one rocket so it could wait in space until needed.

19274.fact: Watched the oceans with a side-looking **radar** that sees through cloud. One satellite like this could image the whole **Russian Arctic** sea in 3 to 5 days.

20103.fact: Nadezhda means **hope**. This was the first one launched under that name: the three before it were hidden behind plain **Kosmos** numbers.

20438.fact: Launched with its sister UoSAT-3 to test new space technology, but it **failed after only two days** and has drifted silently ever since.

20480.fact: Built by the **Japan Amateur Radio League** as a **26-sided** ball covered in solar cells. It stored messages from radio hams and passed them on later.

20692.fact: One of **three Navy spy satellites** flying together. By comparing when a ship’s radio signal reached each one, the trio could **pinpoint where it was**.

21089.fact: A Soviet **Tsikada** navigation satellite with a bonus: it also carried two **amateur radio** relays, called RS-12 and RS-13, for radio hams to use.

21575.fact: Carried copies of the experiments lost when **UoSAT-4 failed** a year earlier, and tested new high-power **gallium arsenide** solar panels.

21809.fact: One of a trio of Navy spy satellites so heavy that they needed a giant **Titan IV** rocket. They tracked ships and could recognise certain **foreign radio systems**.

22078.fact: A test for **S80**, a French plan for satellites to help track and talk to vehicles on the move. The plan was **dropped**, and radiation finally wore this tester out in 1999.

22698.fact: The first satellite to use **GPS to tell which way it was pointing**. Built to last three years, it helped check the aim of military radars until **2013**.

22827.fact: Built for **HealthNet**, which sent medical news to doctors in developing countries. In 1993 it also linked the Canadian icebreaker **Louis S. St-Laurent** in the Northwest Passage.

23125.fact: A **45 cm cube** built by Britain’s defence research agency to test gear in a harsh, high-radiation orbit. Control was later handed to the **University of Colorado**.

23420.fact: Its **Teta** radios used tougher tubes than earlier Molniyas, stretching the planned life to **three years**. It served the military network Korund.

23606.fact: Cerise is French for **cherry**. In 1996 a piece of an old rocket smashed into it, the **first confirmed crash** between two human-made objects in space.

23787.fact: Gonets means **messenger**. One of the first three working Gonets satellites, which were oddly given military **Kosmos** numbers after launch. Later Gonets kept their own name.

24278.fact: The Japan Amateur Radio League’s third satellite, a **26-sided** ball. It rode into space on Japan’s big **H-II rocket** alongside the ADEOS Earth-watching satellite.

24730.fact: Gonets was offered to health groups for sending **medical records** to remote places. It shared its rocket with three military **Strela-3** satellites, its design cousins.

24960.fact: Its two radio antennas sat on **telescopic arms**, and an optical tracker kept one of them aimed at Earth as it swung around its long, looping orbit.

25260.fact: Besides its sharp main camera, it carried **Vegetation**, an instrument that checked on the world’s plant life in strips **2,200 km wide**.

25399.fact: A German **message relay** satellite. Its frequency-hopping trick let **16 ground stations** send data at the same moment on the same channel.

25568.fact: Sweden’s second science microsatellite, built to study the **northern lights**. Contact was lost after 7.5 months, but by then it had sent home a big haul of data.

25731.fact: China’s **first satellite built on a standard bus**, a ready-made body that many missions can share. It also measured space particles and ran a **fluid science** experiment.

25919.fact: Ikonos comes from the Greek word for **image**. It was the first satellite selling pictures to the public that could spot things on the ground just **1 metre** across.

26033.fact: Measured the Sun’s brightness so precisely that it saw sunlight dim by **0.1%** when the planet **Venus passed in front** of the Sun in 2004.

26106.fact: Not a real satellite: a **dummy weight** matching two Cluster science satellites, bolted to a new **Fregat** rocket stage for a test flight months before the real Clusters flew.

26536.fact: Retired after a fault in 2014. A year later it **broke apart in orbit**, scattering more than **200 pieces** of space junk.

26611.fact: Launched with its twin STRV-1c on a big Ariane 5. Within weeks both stopped answering commands, after power to their **radio receivers** was cut off.

26997.fact: Measured the height of the sea surface from space to track ocean currents and **El Niño**. Its name nods to **Jason and the Argonauts**, the Greek heroes on a quest.

27059.fact: A Gonets **messenger** satellite. Its users could carry a **handheld terminal** that looked like a mobile phone to send messages from remote places.

27430.fact: Haiyang means **ocean**. It read the **colour of the sea**, which shows how much algae, mud and pollution the water holds, and watched sea ice too.

27597.fact: Carried five instruments to study Earth’s water and climate, but its **solar panel failed** in October 2003, less than a year into a mission meant to last **at least three years**.

27612.fact: One of the first of a fleet later renamed **AprizeSat**: tiny 12 kg satellites that collected data for **tracking** trucks, ships and other equipment around the world.

27843.fact: Canada’s first space telescope, nicknamed the **Humble Space Telescope** because it was the size of a suitcase. It studied **starquakes** by watching tiny flickers in starlight.

27943.fact: Part of the **Disaster Monitoring Constellation**, in which seven countries shared satellite pictures to help after disasters. Turkish engineers built two of its instruments.

28220.fact: China’s first experimental **digital camera satellite** that could map land in **3D stereo**, a test of technology for later military spy satellites.

28371.fact: A small 35 kg test satellite, built to take pictures sharper than **15 m**. Saudi Arabia’s own **laser station** planned to track its position very precisely.

28470.fact: Officially a civilian **Ziyuan** (“resource”) satellite. It was reportedly part of China’s first sharp-eyed **military camera** series, seeing details 2 m across or less.

28650.fact: One of its two radio relays was built by a **Dutch engineering student**, and the other by Indian radio hams with help from India’s space agency.

28894.fact: A **pan-European student satellite**, about the size of a washing machine. Twenty-three university teams worked together **over the internet**, with ESA’s help, to build it.

29048.fact: One of six Taiwanese and American satellites launched together to gather air data for **weather forecasts**. Designed to last 5 years, they worked for about **14**.

29228.fact: Built from a Russian **spy satellite** design, it could see details under 1 m. Bolted to its side was **PAMELA**, an instrument hunting for **antimatter** in space.

29709.fact: Indonesia’s **first remote sensing satellite**, built with the Technical University of Berlin. Before it, Indonesia had to rely on pictures from **other countries’ satellites**.

31121.fact: One of five 12 kg Saudi **messenger** satellites launched together. They collect messages and deliver them later, and were reportedly the start of a planned **24-satellite** fleet.

31132.fact: A second try: its twin CP2 was lost when the rocket **failed 86 seconds** after liftoff in 2006, so students at **Cal Poly** flew the backup copy instead.

32376.fact: One of four Italian **radar** satellites that can look at the same place **several times a day** in any weather, used for defence and for watching disasters.

32792.fact: Never let go of its rocket: this German experiment stayed **bolted to the rocket’s top stage** in orbit, testing how to pick up ships’ position signals from space.

33315.fact: Nicknamed **Choma**. The five RapidEye satellites flew in a line about **19 minutes apart**, so together they could reach almost any spot on Earth every day.

33409.fact: Shijian 6 satellites flew in **pairs**, officially to study radiation in space. Some experts think they also tested **eavesdropping** technology.

33496.fact: Built by a group of **small factories in Higashiosaka**, near Osaka, to boost local business. It was also meant to watch **thunderstorms** from space.

35499.fact: Strela means **arrow**. Like a **mailbox in orbit**, it stores coded military messages from one ground station and passes them to another later.

35686.fact: AprizeSats weigh just **12 kg**. This one and its twin were the first in the fleet to carry receivers for the **AIS** position signals that ships broadcast.

35936.fact: Not a free-flying satellite: two small German experiments **bolted to a rocket’s top stage**. One studied what happens when ship signals **collide** in busy waters.

36122.fact: Xiwang means **hope**. It was **China’s first amateur radio satellite**, letting radio hams around the world relay voices and messages through it.

36599.fact: The steerable half of a Swedish pair. Mango practised **flying in formation** with its little partner **Tango**, which split off after about two months in orbit.

36799.fact: A 1 kg cube built by students and staff at **SUPSI** in southern Switzerland. It tested how **thin wires** survive atomic oxygen, a corrosive gas found high above Earth.

37179.fact: Launched as a **twin pair** to measure radiation and the space environment. Each Shijian 6 pair was announced with a design life of at least **two years**.

37389.fact: Its camera watched for **forest fires** and **red tides**, blooms of algae that colour the sea. It also tested a set of linked processors working together like a tiny supercomputer.

37791.fact: The **first imaging satellite fully built in Turkey**, designed without know-how from foreign partners. It followed Bilsat-1, whose battery failed in 2006.

37841.fact: Built by students at **SRM University** in Chennai to sniff out **greenhouse gases**. Designed to last one year, it was still working in 2017.

38010.fact: One of four French spy microsatellites flying **a few kilometres apart**. Combining what each one heard let them work out where a radar or radio was.

38338.fact: Named after the Korean folk song **Arirang**. Its camera could see details just **70 cm** across, enough to pick out individual cars.

38735.fact: Renamed **MiR**, short for Mikhail Reshetnev. University students in **Krasnoyarsk** helped build its experiments, including a camera and a laser reflector.

38771.fact: Carries **11 science instruments**, plus two that pass on **distress signals** for search and rescue. It is the middle of three MetOp weather satellites.

39019.fact: Nimble enough to swing quickly and snap several pictures in a row, which can be stitched into one big **mosaic**. It can spot details about **70 cm** across.

39089.fact: The **world’s first space telescope** built to hunt **asteroids** and track satellites. It is about the size of a suitcase.

39159.fact: The V stands for **Vegetation**, not the Roman number five. It watches the world’s plants to help with crop monitoring and **famine prediction**.

39227.fact: **South Korea’s first radar satellite**, able to see the ground on cloudy days and dark nights. It was finished in 2010 but waited **over two years** for its launch.

39260.fact: The first two Fengyun-3 satellites were experiments. This was the **first working model** of China’s second-generation polar weather fleet, weighing about **2,250 kg**.

39417.fact: Tshepiso is the Sesotho word for **promise**. This tiny South African cube carried a radio beacon for **space weather** research.

39425.fact: Later renamed **exactView 12**. It listens for the radio position calls that ships make, so their positions can be gathered from space, even far out at sea.

39438.fact: Velox is Latin for **swift**. This 1 kg cube was the **first CubeSat** of Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University, built by undergraduate students.

39452.fact: One of three Swarm satellites mapping Earth’s **magnetic field**. Two fly side by side and one flies higher, together giving a view of **Earth’s insides** from space.

39491.fact: Just a metal ball: a **radar calibration sphere** that ground radars track to check their aim. It rode on the **first flight** of the Soyuz-2-1v rocket.

39761.fact: Part of a newer **Strela** military messenger series also called Rodnik. Store-and-forward relays like it are handy where there are **no phone lines** or cables.

40010.fact: Can photograph **1 million square km** of land a day, in strips 77 km wide, and tilt its camera up to **38 degrees** sideways to reach places off its path.

40018.fact: Changed hands twice: first renamed **exactView 11**, then in 2020 sold to **Myriota** to carry messages for the Internet of Things.

40034.fact: **Uruguay’s first satellite**, built by university engineering students with the national phone company ANTEL. It carried colour and **infrared** cameras.

40055.fact: Twin of CanX-5. The two tiny Canadian satellites practised **formation flying**, using GPS to measure the gap between them to within about **10 cm**.

40070.fact: Relek is short for **relativistic electrons**, super-fast particles it was sent to study. Renamed Vernov after a Soviet physicist, it went silent after just **five months**.

40110.fact: One of three Chinese satellites flying as a team, thought to work like the US Navy’s spy trios: listening for **ships’ radio signals** to find them at sea.

40261.fact: Its purpose was **never disclosed**. Experts guess the Shijian 11 fleet may watch for **missile launches** or listen in on radio signals.

40340.fact: Part of the fifth trio of these Chinese satellites. Flying in a tight group about **1,100 km** up, they are believed to track **ships** by their radio signals.

40555.fact: Believed to be the third of a secretive Russian series whose satellites **manoeuvred close** to their own rocket stages. It began manoeuvring a few weeks after launch.

40878.fact: The fifth of a generation of Chinese **optical spy satellites** that began with Yaogan 8 in 2009. Each weighs about **1,040 kg**.

40958.fact: A **test satellite** for trying out Chinese-made camera chips. It was one of the **first four Jilin-1** satellites, and also carried a radio for amateurs.

41099.fact: A **15.8 kg** radar target ball for Almaz-Antey, a maker of anti-aircraft systems. The main satellite on its rocket **failed to separate**, but this ball got out fine.

41339.fact: Nicknamed **Kinshachi 3** and built by two Nagoya universities. It listened for ships and carried an **infrared camera** to spot space junk.

41603.fact: Also called **LAPAN-ORARI**, it was shared with Indonesia’s radio hams: besides taking pictures, it carried a **voice repeater** they could talk through.

41783.fact: Built by students at **IIT Bombay** to count electrons in the upper air, which could make **GPS more accurate** in India. Its beacon was heard, but its data link never was.

41849.fact: Measured heat and light leaving Earth with a **forest of carbon nanotubes**, so black they soak up almost all light, inside a sensor the size of a **deck of cards**.

41885.fact: One of eight NASA **hurricane** watchers. It measures ocean winds by catching **GPS signals bounced off the sea**, and with panels open it is about the size of a **swan**.

41899.fact: Its name has never been officially confirmed. Weighing just **66 kg**, it rode into space beside China’s **TanSat** and two small Spark satellites.

43016.fact: A **3D-printed** satellite from a small university in Idaho, testing how different **plastics** survive in space. It paved the way for a sister satellite printed aboard the space station.

44408.fact: Tested a thruster that heats **water into plasma** to push a spacecraft. Only 3 of its 23 firings made any plasma, and contact was lost after **three months**.

46458.fact: Launched from a **ship at sea** with eight sister satellites. These Jilin-1 satellites weigh around **42 kg** yet can spot details smaller than 1 m.

48951.fact: Tested a **refuelling port** and two kinds of thrusters, one burning hydrogen peroxide, to practise the moves needed for future satellites to **meet and dock**.

51053.fact: Built by a Norwegian university to spot **harmful algal blooms** in the ocean, using a camera that splits light into many narrow **colours**.

53445.fact: Nicknamed **Xi’an Hangtou 1**. It shared one rocket with **15 other Jilin-1 satellites**, all released into orbit together.

54252.fact: Jilin-1 is named after **Jilin Province**, home of the company that runs it. It is China’s **largest commercial satellite fleet**.

55056.fact: A **space tug** from the company Momentus, built to carry small satellites to new orbits. Its thrusters use **water** heated by microwaves instead of normal rocket fuel.

56204.fact: Nicknamed **Mey-Lin**: GHGSat names its satellites after **team members’ children**. It hunts for leaks of **methane**, a powerful greenhouse gas.

58019.fact: One of three small Spanish satellites meant to work as a team, checking **water quality in reservoirs**. Their team leader **failed to deploy** from the rocket.

58304.fact: One of **36 SuperDoves** launched together, alongside Planet’s first **Pelican** test satellite, to help photograph Earth’s land every day.

58820.fact: Nicknamed **Mofulong**. It was one of five satellites from the company Minospace that rode into space together on a single **Kinetica-1** rocket.

59289.fact: A Navy school satellite testing a **terahertz camera**, which sees a kind of light between microwaves and infrared, plus a radio built in **New Zealand**.

60556.fact: Also called **SASAT 1**. Its camera sees **45 colours** of light to study crops and forests, and it collects data from sensors on the ground about rain and **bushfires**.

61773.fact: One of many SITRO-AIS cubesats built by the company **SPUTNIX**. It listens for the **position calls** that ships broadcast and relays them to the ground.

61788.fact: Helps keep shipping **safe** by collecting ships’ AIS position signals from space. **24 SITRO-AIS** satellites rode up on this one Soyuz launch.

62644.fact: Launched after the original ANSER Leader **failed to deploy** in 2023. The leader’s job is to command a team of small Spanish satellites and carry a **mini camera**.

65267.fact: Launched with three near-identical satellites on an **Angara** rocket. Experts believe they are **spy satellites** with cameras, each weighing around 520 kg.

67253.fact: Works as a **pair** with Aist-2T 2, taking **3D stereo pictures** of Earth to map the land and watch for **fires, floods and volcanoes**.

67688.fact: Nicknamed **Teruteru**, this tiny cube from the Hokkaido University of Science was released from the space station to **flash messages** toward Earth with LEDs.

69648.fact: Built by Tohoku, Hokkaido and Muroran universities to test **deep-space** gear close to home, including a small, efficient thruster, for future trips **beyond the Moon**.

100089.fact: Part of **Bureau 1440**’s plan for Russian satellite internet. These satellites talk to each other with **lasers** and steer using electric thrusters fed with krypton gas.

facts: From the **Kosmos** rocket family. Its main version, the Kosmos-3M, flew **more than 440 times** between 1967 and 2010.
The rocket’s first stage began as the **R-14**, a Soviet missile built to carry a nuclear warhead, turned into a satellite launcher.
Kosmos-3M second stages burned **UDMH and nitric acid**, two liquids that catch fire the instant they touch, so no spark is needed.
A Kosmos-3M second stage could **fire its engine twice**: once to reach space, then again later to round out its orbit.
A single Kosmos-3M could drop off **eight small satellites** on one launch, spacing them out around the same orbit.
Most of these rockets launched from **Plesetsk**, a military cosmodrome in the forests of northern Russia that was kept secret for years.
In 1975 a Kosmos-3M launched **Aryabhata**, India’s very first satellite, from Kapustin Yar, a launch site near the Volga River.
An empty stage **can tumble** as it orbits. Sunlight glinting off its changing angles may make it brighten and fade as you watch.
This is the third stage of a **Tsyklon-3**, a rocket that flew **122 times** from 1977 to 2009, always from Plesetsk in northern Russia.
Tsyklon-3 grew out of the **R-36**, one of the biggest nuclear missiles the Soviet Union ever built.
This third stage could **restart its engine** in space, letting it fine-tune a satellite’s orbit before letting go.
All three stages burned **nitrogen tetroxide and UDMH**, toxic fuels that ignite on contact. That toxicity helped get the rocket retired.
In 2013 Ecuador’s **Pegaso** satellite began tumbling after a close pass by one of these stages. Its operators suspected a strike by nearby debris; a collision was not confirmed.
One Tsyklon-3 stage has **broken apart five times** because of leftover fuel inside, scattering more than 100 pieces of debris.
A Tsyklon-3 could carry **six satellites at once**, a trick used to launch Soviet military communication satellites in batches.
The whole rocket stood about **39 metres tall**, as high as a 13-storey building, and was built by Yuzhmash in Dnipro, Ukraine.
From an **Ariane 5**, Europe’s heavy-lift rocket, which flew **117 times** between 1996 and 2023.
Ariane 5 launched the **James Webb Space Telescope** so precisely that Webb saved enough fuel to possibly double its working life.
Ariane 5’s upper stage is **5.4 metres wide** but less than 5 metres tall, so it looks more like a giant drum than a rocket.
From 2003 to 2017, Ariane 5 pulled off **82 successful launches in a row** without a single failure.
It launched from **Kourou in French Guiana**, close to the equator, where Earth’s spin gives rockets a free push eastward.
Ariane 5 often carried **two big satellites** at once, one stacked above the other inside its nose cone.
Ariane 5 sent **Rosetta** on its 10-year trip to a comet, where its lander Philae made the first landing on a comet’s surface.
Most of this rocket was built in Europe and **shipped by boat** across the Atlantic Ocean to its launch site in South America.
From one of Europe’s first Ariane rockets. **Ariane 1** first flew on Christmas Eve 1979, giving Europe its own ride to space.
This third stage burned **liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen**. Hydrogen stays liquid only when chilled below about minus 253°C.
By early 1986, the first Ariane rockets **led the world market** for launching commercial satellites.
Ariane 1, 2 and 3 flew **28 times** in total, all from Kourou in French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America.
The **Ariane 40** was the plainest Ariane 4, with **no strap-on boosters** at all, just its three stages stacked up.
From an **Ariane 4**, which flew **116 times** from 1988 to 2003 and won about half of all commercial satellite launches.
From an **Ariane 6**, Europe’s new heavy-lift rocket. Its upper stage’s **Vinci engine** burns hydrogen and can restart several times in space.
From a **Delta** rocket, a family that grew out of the **Thor** nuclear missile and began launching satellites in 1960.
Delta got its name because it was the **fourth** upper stage tried on the Thor missile, and delta is the fourth Greek letter.
In 1964 a Delta launched **Syncom 3**, the first communications satellite to hover over one spot on the equator.
Japan built its own **licensed copies** of the Delta rocket and used them to launch Japanese satellites from 1975 to 1992.
NASA planned Delta as a **stopgap** rocket for 1960 and 1961. The family ended up flying for **64 years**.
The Delta family flew **more than 300 times** between 1960 and 2024, with a 95% success rate.
From a **Delta II**, a rocket that flew 155 times between 1989 and 2018. It launched the Mars rovers **Spirit and Opportunity**.
Delta II was built to launch **GPS satellites** after the 1986 Challenger disaster moved them off the Space Shuttle.
Delta II launched **Mars Pathfinder** and the **Kepler** telescope, which found thousands of planets circling other stars.
Its first stage was ringed with up to **nine solid boosters** that lit and dropped away in groups as they burned out.
Delta II fell short only **twice** in 155 launches: one failure in 1997 and one partial failure in 1995.
Delta II’s optional third stage was a **spinning solid motor** that twirled like a top to keep itself pointed straight.
From a **Delta IV**, which flew **45 times** from 2002 to 2024. Its heavy version launched the Parker Solar Probe toward the Sun.
This stage’s **RL10 engine** has a nozzle extension that slides out after separation, like a telescope, to squeeze more push from its hydrogen fuel.
This small object is a **SOZ ullage motor**, a booster pack that rode on the upper stage of a Soviet or Russian **Proton** rocket.
Its job: give a gentle push before the main engine restarts, so the floating fuel **settles to the bottom** of the tanks.
Each Proton upper stage carried **two** of these motor packs and dropped them once their work was done.
Leftover fuel makes these little motors risky: **dozens have exploded** in orbit years later, creating clouds of debris.
From a **Proton**, a Soviet and Russian heavy rocket that has launched **more than 400 times** since 1965.
Proton launched the **Zarya and Zvezda** modules, the first Russian pieces of the International Space Station.
From a **Proton**, a Soviet and Russian heavy rocket that has launched **more than 400 times** since 1965.
Proton launched the **Zarya and Zvezda** modules, the first Russian pieces of the International Space Station.
This is the third stage of a **Long March 4C**, a three-stage Chinese rocket that has flown **more than 55 times** since 2006.
Unlike the older Long March 4B, this third stage can **restart its engines** in space to fine-tune a satellite’s orbit.
All three stages burn **nitrogen tetroxide and UDMH**, fuels that can sit in the tanks at room temperature, ready to launch.
This third stage is pushed by **two small engines** side by side, called YF-40s, instead of one big one.
Long March 4C rockets launch **weather and radar satellites**, such as China’s Fengyun-3 and Yaogan series.
Long March rockets are named after the **Long March**, the Chinese Red Army’s long retreat across China in 1934 and 1935.
From a **Vostok** rocket, part of the same R-7 family that launched Yuri Gagarin, the first person in space.
The Vostok-2M version of this rocket flew **93 times** from 1964 to 1991, and only one of those launches failed.
This third stage is called **Blok E**. R-7 stages are named after letters: the core is Blok A and the four boosters are B, V, G and D.
Most Vostok-2M rockets carried **Meteor weather satellites**, sending them into orbits that pass close to both poles.
Blok E burned **kerosene and liquid oxygen**, the same fuel mix as the rest of the rocket below it.
The final Vostok-2M flew in 1991 carrying an **Indian satellite**, ending the rocket line that had carried Gagarin.
This is an **Electron kick stage**, a tiny third stage that gives satellites a final nudge into exactly the right orbit.
Its **Curie engine** is 3D printed and can fire several times, so one kick stage can drop satellites in different places.
Electron’s main engines were the first on an orbital rocket to use **battery-powered electric pumps** to push their fuel.
Most Electrons launch from Rocket Lab’s own site on the **Mahia Peninsula** in New Zealand.
Rocket Lab gives its launches playful names, like **It’s Business Time** and This One’s For Pickering.
Electron is built from light **carbon fibre** and has flown more than 90 times since 2017, making it one of the busiest small rockets.
From a **Falcon 9**, SpaceX’s two-stage rocket. It has carried **hundreds of missions** into orbit, from small satellites to crews bound for the space station.
Falcon 9’s first stage lands to fly again, but the **second stage is not reused**. This one was left in orbit after its job.
This second stage runs on a single **Merlin Vacuum** engine, burning rocket-grade kerosene and liquid oxygen.
In 2020 Falcon 9 became the **first commercial rocket to carry astronauts** into orbit.
A Falcon 9 booster first landed itself in **December 2015**. Some boosters have since flown more than 30 times.

From the **first PSLV to succeed**. The very first PSLV test flight had failed the year before, but India’s rocket has flown dozens of times since.
From **Black Arrow**, the rocket behind the UK’s **only successful orbital launch** on its own rocket, fired from Woomera in Australia.
From a **Mu-3H**, one of Japan’s solid-fuel **Mu** rockets. The Mu family flew from Uchinoura between **1966 and 2006**, carrying many of Japan’s early science missions.
From a **Kuaizhou-11**, a bigger member of China’s **quick-reaction** Kuaizhou family, able to carry about 1,500 kg to low orbit.
From North Korea’s **Chollima-1**, named after a **mythical winged horse**. Its first stage is thought to come from a North Korean missile.
From a South Korean **solid-fuel** test rocket that launched from a **barge at sea**, about 4 km south of Jeju Island.
Left from an Iranian **Simorgh** launch. Simorgh is a two-stage rocket named after a **giant mythical bird** of Persian legend.
A **Yuanzheng-1S** upper stage, a simplified member of a family whose name means **“expedition”**. It helps place satellites into their intended orbits.
From an **LVM3**, India’s heavy rocket, which launched the **Chandrayaan-2 and 3** Moon missions. A human-rated version was developed for **Gaganyaan**.
From a **Long March 2F**, the rocket that launches Chinese astronauts. It has flown every crewed **Shenzhou** mission.
From a **Long March 12B**, a 4.4-metre-wide Chinese rocket whose nine-engine first stage is designed to **land and fly again**.
From a **Long March 10B**, a commercial member of the Long March 10 family, the rockets China is building to send **astronauts to the Moon**.
From a **Gravity-1**, the world’s most powerful **solid-fuel** orbital rocket when it debuted, launched from a ship in the Yellow Sea.
From a **Yinli-1**, also called Gravity-1. It uses **seven solid rocket motors**: four light on the ground and three fire later in flight.
